title: 1-carat polished up 0.5% in August, first rise in 15 months
dek: Rapaport's index shows small rounds leading the recovery, with the 0.30-carat up 2% and the 0.50-carat up 2.5%. The 3-carat slipped 0.4% after 18 months without a move.
body: The one-carat polished index rose in August. The Rapaport Trade Diamond Index for 1-carat round D to H, IF to VS2 goods gained 0.5% across the month, which Rapaport describes as its first increase in fifteen months, following readings that were flat or negative going back to May 2025. The release was published in New York on 2 September at 08:21 UTC. Below it, the 0.30-carat index gained 2% and the 0.50-carat 2.5%, both continuing a rebound this desk has been tracking since July. RAPI measures asking prices, not settled trades: it is the average asking price of the cheapest tenth of round diamonds in each of the top twenty-five quality categories listed on Rapaport Trade, the marketplace formerly called RapNet, which carries more than $8 billion of daily listings.

The category that turned is the three-carat, and it turned the other way. It slipped 0.4% in August after what Rapaport calls a year and a half of steadiness. That matters against what this paper printed on 4 August, when July was reported here as the first month since March 2025 in which none of the four headline sizes fell. That condition lasted exactly one month. Compounded across the two months, the 0.30-carat is up 3.63%, the 0.50-carat 4.35%, the 1-carat 0.50% and the 3-carat down 0.20%, on this desk's arithmetic from Rapaport's own monthly figures. The spread between the best and worst size over two months is 4.55 percentage points, and it is the small goods that are carrying it.

Rapaport attributes the recovery to supply, not to a return of demand: miners and manufacturers cut production, and the categories that fell hardest in 2025 rebounded as the imbalance closed. Trading picked up after the summer slowdown, round stones outperformed fancies, and Indian manufacturers shipped to the United States once the July confirmation of a 10% tariff rate on Indian goods removed an uncertainty this paper reported on 2 August. Business at the India International Jewellery Show in Mumbai is described as brisk. Antwerp and Israel were seasonally quiet, and Chinese demand was slow ahead of the September Jewellery and Gem World fair in Hong Kong. One further reason is given for the 1 to 1.49-carat band specifically: falling inventory, and reports of consumers cooling on lab-grown stones.

What has not been repaired sits in the same release. Rapaport notes miners still reporting sales declines, citing Alrosa's first-half revenue down 36% year on year to 74.16 billion roubles, or $901.6 million, with a loss of 10.67 billion roubles, and De Beers' first-half revenue down 19% to $1.58 billion. Both sets of figures were reported by this paper when they were published, on 6 August and 31 July respectively, and neither is new today. Our own tape carries the RAPI 1.00-carat level at 3,881.34, a July 2026 point that is provisional and has not been revised since the last read, so it does not yet carry August's 0.5%. A monthly index is a monthly index, and this paper marks it as one rather than pretending it moves daily.

The desk's view: a half point is a small number and it is the right size for what happened. Fifteen months of the one-carat not rising is the fact that has organised every polished conversation since the middle of last year, and it has ended on supply discipline rather than on buyers arriving, which is the same engine that produced July. A jeweller restocking for the holidays should read the 0.30 to 0.69 band as genuinely firmer and the three-carat as the size where the estimate book now needs checking, because eighteen months of steadiness ending is a change in a number that had stopped being watched. The test is the same one this desk named on 4 August and it is now days away: Vicenzaoro opens tomorrow and Hong Kong follows, and September is when the asking prices in this index meet budgets.

title: $119.30 back on gold: the first higher mark since 28 August
dek: Gold $4,426.80, silver $65.58, platinum $1,762.00, palladium $1,348.00 at 05:59 ET, every one higher. Gold recovers 40.17% of the $297.00 it lost after 28 August, and stays $177.70 below that mark.
body: All four metals were re-read off the Kitco board at 05:59 ET this morning, all four had moved off the 05:00 mark, and all four were written back to the tape before this edition built. Gold $4,426.80 the ounce, up $39.80 or 0.9072% on the prior close of $4,387.00; silver $65.58, up $0.37 or 0.5674%; platinum $1,762.00, up $6.00 or 0.3417%; palladium $1,348.00, up $13.00 or 0.9738%. Against this paper's own marks of record yesterday that is gold up $119.30 or 2.7696%, silver up $2.02 or 3.1781%, platinum up $49.00 or 2.8605% and palladium up $62.00 or 4.8212%. The gold-silver ratio is 67.50 against 67.77 yesterday. Every figure here is a Kitco bid, the convention this tape uses for all four metals.

The run that ended is worth counting rather than describing. Gold has been marked on this tape at $4,604.50 on 28 August, $4,454.40 on the 29th, $4,454.40 again on Sunday the 30th, $4,444.80 on the 31st, $4,366.10 on 1 September and $4,307.50 on the 2nd. That is four lower marks across five tape entries, with the fifth a Sunday carrying Saturday's reading forward unchanged. Today is the first higher mark since 28 August. It recovers $119.30 of the $297.00 the ounce lost across that span, or 40.17% of it, and leaves gold $177.70, or 3.8593%, below where this tape carried it on 28 August. No source read this morning named a cause for the move and none is asserted here.

The second page agrees. CNBC's quote service, read at 06:02 ET, returned $4,426.78 for gold against a Kitco midpoint of $4,427.80, a gap of 0.0230%; $65.6287 for silver against a midpoint of $65.705, 0.1161%; $1,766.28 for platinum against $1,767.00, 0.0407%; and $1,364.96 for palladium against $1,368.00, 0.2222%. Every one of those comparisons is a midpoint against a last price, which is the like-for-like test this desk adopted after August's palladium episode rather than setting a bid against a mid. All four sit inside the agreement band, so there is no outside-source divergence to disclose this session.

Palladium is the metal to look at twice, for the same reason it was in August. Kitco quotes it $1,348.00 bid against a $1,388.00 ask, a gap of $40.00, or 2.9674% of the bid. The metal gained $13.00 on the day. The cost of crossing its own spread is therefore just over three times the day's move, which is a liquidity fact rather than a price fact, and it is the fourth consecutive session on which this paper has marked a $40 palladium spread. A correction printed elsewhere in today's edition revises the length of that metal's August hold from nine sessions to seven tape entries; the spread arithmetic that resolved the hold was correct then and is unchanged now.

The desk's view: one higher mark is not a turn, and this desk will not call it one. What can be said is narrower and more useful. Gold has retraced two fifths of a six-day fall in a single reading, silver and palladium have retraced more of theirs in percentage terms, and the whole complex moved together in the same direction on the same morning, which is the shape of a positioning move rather than a story about any one metal. A retailer repricing off the board should note that the ounce is still $177.70 below where it stood a week ago and that the wholesale ticket has not caught up with either direction yet.

title: IIGJ and IIT Madras split 90 hours, and 60 of them are physics
dek: The Indian Institute of Gems & Jewellery and IIT Madras's InCent-LGD centre launched a 90-hour hybrid certificate on 2 September. Sixty of the ninety hours are IIT Madras's, and only twelve are on campus.
body: India has put a syllabus behind its lab-grown programme. The Indian Institute of Gems and Jewellery, which is supported by the Gem and Jewellery Export Promotion Council, has launched a Certificate in Lab-Grown Diamond Technology with the India Centre for Lab-Grown Diamond at IIT Madras, known as InCent-LGD. The programme runs 90 hours in a hybrid format across evening and weekend sessions. It was announced on 2 September at 05:35 UTC in Solitaire, the council's own magazine, and this is a single-source item: no independent trade pickup was found by this paper's overnight desk or on a repeat check this morning. It is printed because the source is the announcing body itself, which is the standing of a company release rather than a third-party claim.

The split is the number worth carrying. IIGJ delivers 30 of the 90 hours, all live online, covering the global diamond industry, the emergence of lab-grown goods, market and consumer fundamentals, entrepreneurship, trade and exports, regulatory frameworks and a strategic outlook. IIT Madras delivers the other 60: 48 hours live online and 12 hours of campus immersion. Its half of the curriculum is materials science and process engineering, listing graphite and diamond structures, high pressure high temperature growth, microwave plasma chemical vapour deposition, growth through MPCVD, post-processing and advanced characterisation. Two thirds of the course is therefore the physics of making the stone, a third is the business of selling it, and 13.33% of the total is in a room.

What is not published is worth stating plainly rather than leaving as an absence. The announcement carries no fee, no cohort size, no start date, no admission requirement and no statement of accreditation or credit weighting. It gives an email address and a telephone number and nothing else that can be priced. This desk has not found a second document carrying any of it. A trade paper can report the structure of a course exactly, because 30 plus 48 plus 12 is checkable arithmetic, and cannot report its cost or its scale, because neither has been said.

The context is this paper's own reporting, on both sides. On 25 August this desk reported InCent-LGD's prototype high pressure press at IIT Madras, built under a 242 crore rupee research programme, with large components for a full-scale commercial machine shipped in for assembly. That was hardware. This is the people to run it, from the same centre, seven weeks into the same programme. The price backdrop is less comfortable. Our tape carries the one-carat lab-grown reference at $676 this morning, a dollar above yesterday, and Rapaport's August price release, reported elsewhere in today's edition, names consumers cooling on lab-grown stones as one reason natural goods in the 1 to 1.49-carat band steadied.

The desk's view: training capacity is the least reversible thing a country can build in this trade and it is being built for a product whose price has been falling for two years. Those two facts are not in conflict. India's exposure to lab-grown is manufacturing exposure, not retail margin, and 60 hours of MPCVD and characterisation is a bet on being the place that grows and processes the material at cost rather than the place that sells it at a premium. A jeweller reading this from the retail side should take one thing from it: the supply of people who understand how these stones are made is about to increase, and the technical scarcity that supported early margins is not what it was.

title: $297.00 off gold and $170.00 off platinum: every mark lower since Friday
dek: Gold $4,307.50 and platinum $1,713.00 at press time, the fifth consecutive lower mark for each on this tape. Gold has given up 6.45% since 28 August, platinum 9.03%, and silver more than either at 9.68%.
body: All four metals were re-read off the Kitco board at press time on Wednesday and all four were lower. Gold $4,307.50 the ounce, down $20.20 or 0.4668% on the prior close. Platinum $1,713.00, down $24.00 or 1.3817%. Silver $63.56, down $0.394 or 0.6161%. Palladium $1,286.00, down $1.00 or 0.0777%, which on a board this size is flat. Every one of those readings differed from the 05:00 mark, and every one has been written back to this paper's tape before this edition built, so the numbers printed here are the numbers the tape carries. A second page was read for gold: Trading Economics had spot at $4,305.69, 0.065% off Kitco's midpoint, which is inside the band and leaves nothing to disclose.

The session itself is unremarkable. The run behind it is not. Gold has printed a lower mark on this tape at every reading since Friday 28 August: $4,604.50, then $4,454.40, then $4,444.80, then $4,366.10, and now $4,307.50. That is $297.00 off the ounce, 6.45%, across five marks. Platinum has done the same thing without a single higher reading in between, $1,883.00 down to $1,713.00, a fall of $170.00 or 9.03%. Silver and palladium each managed one higher mark on the way, so neither run is unbroken, but both metals are materially lower across the span.

Rank the four by what they have lost since 28 August and the order is not the one the headlines imply. Silver is worst at 9.68%, from $70.37 to $63.56. Platinum follows at 9.03%. Palladium has lost 6.88%, from $1,381.00 to $1,286.00. Gold, the metal everyone is watching, has lost the least of the four at 6.45%. The gold-silver ratio sits at 67.77 against 65.43 on 28 August, so an ounce of gold buys 2.34 more ounces of silver than it did five marks ago. The platinum-palladium ratio has gone the other way, 1.363 to 1.332, because palladium has barely moved this session while platinum took the largest percentage fall of the four.

On the cause this desk prints the direction and withholds the contested number, as it did on Tuesday. Trading Economics, read this morning, attributes the pressure to rising Treasury yields and to expectations of a Federal Reserve rate rise. Outside estimates of the September probability still differ by more than twenty points across the outlets this desk reads, so no probability is printed here. What is not in dispute is the arithmetic on a cost sheet. A retailer who bought casting gold against the 28 August ounce is carrying stock priced $297.00 above today's metal, and a retailer buying this week is buying 6.45% cheaper than one who bought last Friday.

The desk's view: five marks is a run, not yet a trend, and the useful reading is which metals fell together rather than how far gold fell. When silver and platinum lose nine per cent while gold loses six, the trade is selling the whole complex and not expressing a view on any one of them. For the bench that matters more than the gold number, because platinum at $1,713.00 and silver at $63.56 reset the cost of every setting and every chain in the case, not only the yellow ones. Price the case off today's board, not off the week the metal was bought.

title: $675 for the one-carat while the index rises $12: lab-grown splits in two
dek: CaratRadar's one-carat average fell $12 to $675, a third straight lower mark from Monday's $700. Its whole-market index rose $12 to $1,535 over the same day, and active listings passed 1.21 million.
body: CaratRadar's page, read directly by this desk at press time, puts the one-carat lab-grown average at $675 as of 2 September. That is $12 below Tuesday's $687 and $25 below Monday's $700, a fall of 3.57% across three readings. This paper reported on Tuesday that the $13 step from $700 to $687 was the largest single-day move the reference had made since this tape opened on 5 August, when every prior move had been three dollars or less. It has now been followed by a $12 step in the same direction.

The more interesting number is the one moving the other way. The same page puts the market price index at $1,535 on 2 September against $1,523 on 1 September, a rise of $12 or 0.79%. The one-carat average and the whole-market index moved by the same twelve dollars, on the same day, in opposite directions. The index spans every size and grade on the marketplace. The one-carat average spans one size. The two diverge when the mix moves, not when the market falls as a whole, and on this reading the mix is what moved.

Supply is the third figure and it points the same way. Active listings went from 1,204,718 on 1 September to 1,211,846 on 2 September, 7,128 more stones in a day, up 0.59%. Listed prices run from $51 to $1,503,988. More goods on offer while the average asking price at one specific size falls is the ordinary shape of a segment clearing inventory. It is a different condition from a market repricing across the board, and the two should not be reported as the same event.

One caution on reading these numbers against this paper's own price chip. The LGD1 chip on the tape is drawn from a separate wholesale file and prints the midpoint of a CVD wholesale band, $475.00, dated 30 July 2026 on that file. CaratRadar's $675 is an average of asking prices across a marketplace of live listings, read today. They are not the same measurement, they are not from the same week, and they should not be netted against one another. A listings average tells you what sellers are asking. A wholesale band midpoint tells you roughly what the trade pays.

The desk's view: three lower marks in a row at the one-carat point, against a whole-market index that rose on the same day, is not a collapse and should not be sold to a customer as one. What it is, on this evidence, is a one-carat segment carrying more stock than it can clear at last week's asking prices while the rest of the marketplace holds. The practical consequence for a retailer is narrow and immediate. The one-carat lab-grown stone in the case is being asked for less than it was on Monday, and nothing on this page says the same is true of the sizes sitting beside it.

title: £59,000 in Penzance: a steel Patek beats its low estimate 11.8 times
dek: A stainless Calatrava reference 448, found during a Cornish house clearance, sold at Hansons on 25 August against a £5,000 to £10,000 estimate. The winning bid came by telephone from Hong Kong.
body: A stainless steel Patek Philippe and Co Calatrava, reference 448, sold for £59,000 at Hansons Cornwall in Penzance on 25 August. The watch was found in a jewellery box during a house clearance in Camborne after the owner's death, and had passed within the same family for decades as a gift from a grandmother to her husband. The auctioneer records serial number 822731 and case number 610667, and dates the watch to the 1930s. The buyer bid by telephone from Hong Kong. The result was picked up by the trade press on 31 August and 1 September.

The estimate was £5,000 to £10,000. Against the lower bound the result is 11.8 times. Against the upper bound it is 5.9 times, and both figures belong in the record, because quoting only the first is how a saleroom result turns into a headline rather than a number. The dollar equivalents reported around the sale do not agree with one another: National Jeweler carried $79,892 and the syndicated wire copy carried $78,765 for the same £59,000, implying conversion rates of 1.3541 and 1.3350. This paper prints the pound, which is the currency the sale was struck in. None of the reports state whether £59,000 is the hammer price or includes the buyer's premium.

The scarcity argument belongs to the auctioneer and it is the ordinary one for this material. Hansons' senior valuer put the interest down to how few stainless steel watches Patek Philippe made in the period, which leaves surviving examples thin on the ground. The house also reports that the watch was still running when it arrived, after roughly nine decades in one Cornish family. Bidding is described as international, with competition from Japan and China before the telephone line from Hong Kong took it.

The result lands in an unusually empty stretch of the calendar, which is worth stating rather than glossing. This desk checked the salerooms this morning. Sotheby's next jewellery sales are The Gem Drop in New York from 14 to 17 September and High Jewelry in Hong Kong on 17 September. Bonhams closed jewellery sales on 1 and 2 September and publishes no totals for either. A £59,000 lot from a regional Cornish room is, at present, the most substantial dated jewellery or watch auction figure this desk could find among the houses it checked this morning.

Correction, 3 September 2026: an earlier version of this article called the £59,000 Calatrava the most substantial dated jewellery or watch auction figure available to print anywhere in the trade. The paragraph disclosed a check of two houses, Sotheby's and Bonhams, which is not the whole trade, and the sentence is narrowed here to what was actually checked. This paper's standards desk searched independently on 2 September for a larger dated total in the same window, across Christie's, Phillips and Heritage, and found none, so the claim may well have been true; the fault was the scope it asserted rather than the number it rested on. Every figure in the piece, including both dollar conversions and both estimate multiples, was correct as published.

The desk's view: the number worth carrying out of Penzance is not £59,000, it is £5,000. That was a professional valuation on a watch that made almost twelve times it, which says the reference material for mid-century steel Patek is thinner than the estimate assumed. A jeweller holding estate stock, or writing valuations off a book more than a year or two old, should read this as a pricing problem rather than as a good story about a lucky family. The stock in the back room is being valued against the same tables that produced the £5,000.

title: Two CEOs and a president: Kering rewires Pomellato, DoDo and its Italian holding
dek: Charlotte Fournet takes Pomellato and Krizia Cucurachi takes DoDo on 15 September, both reporting to Jean-Marc Duplaix. Sabina Belli, Pomellato's chief since 2015, becomes president of Kering Italia.
body: Kering named Charlotte Fournet chief executive of Pomellato and Krizia Cucurachi chief executive of DoDo on 1 September, both appointments effective 15 September. Both report to Jean-Marc Duplaix, the group's chief operating officer, who also runs the jewellery division. On the same date Sabina Belli, who has led Pomellato since 2015, becomes president of Kering Italia, the group's Italian holding. Three moves, one date, and they are best read as a single reorganisation of the group's Italian jewellery base rather than as three separate hirings.

Fournet arrives with fourteen years inside the group's own houses. She joined Saint Laurent in 2014, moved to Gucci in 2019 and to Bottega Veneta in 2020, working in merchandising and product strategy. Her stated brief at Pomellato is elevated branding, higher store productivity and wider distribution, which is a mandate about the shape of the retail estate rather than about design. Cucurachi's brief at DoDo is narrower and clearer still: strategic development, with the house positioned around jewellery bought as a gift.

Belli's move upward is the part with the most weight behind it. Eleven years at the head of Pomellato covers the period in which the house became the larger of Kering's two Milanese jewellers, and the presidency of Kering Italia puts her across the group's whole Italian operation rather than one maison. The company has not published financial responsibilities attached to the role and this desk has not seen a figure for it, so no scope is claimed here beyond the title.

The context is this paper's own reporting from 29 July. Kering's jewellery houses, Boucheron, Pomellato, Qeelin and DoDo, lifted first-half revenue to 521 million euros, up 14% as reported and 20% on a comparable basis, with operating income doubling to 32 million euros. Group revenue over the same half fell 3% to 7.22 billion euros. The jewellery division was created in March of this year and handed to Duplaix. Putting new chief executives into two of its four houses six months later is what a group does with the part of the portfolio that is growing, not the part it is fixing.

The desk's view: personnel news is usually the thinnest kind of trade story, and this one is worth reading only because of where it sits in the accounts. Kering's jewellery is a 521 million euro business inside a 7.22 billion euro group that shrank, and it is the piece the group is now staffing up and giving an Italian corporate spine. For jewellers who stock or compete with Pomellato and DoDo, the near-term signal is distribution: a mandate written around store productivity and wider distribution usually shows up first as more doors, then as pressure on the ones already open.

title: $24,900 for a rubber Big Bang: Hublot prices texture as a material, not a finish
dek: The Big Bang Original Soft Touch launched on 1 September in All Black and All Red at $24,900, on the in-house HUB1280 column-wheel chronograph built at Nyon.
body: Hublot introduced the Big Bang Original Soft Touch on 1 September at $24,900. The watch runs the in-house HUB1280 column-wheel chronograph, conceived, developed and assembled at the company's manufacture in Nyon, and comes in two colourways, All Black and All Red. It is the first watch this desk has recorded from the house in which the selling point is neither the movement nor the case metal but the surface of the rubber.

The technical claim is specific enough to be checkable, which is more than most launch copy manages. The textured compound is overmoulded, meaning the texture is embedded during manufacture rather than applied afterwards as a coating or a surface treatment, and it runs across case, bezel, dial and strap rather than the strap alone. The company's argument is that this keeps the durability and resistance associated with a rubber component while changing how it feels. A coating wears off a bezel. A material property does not, and that is the whole of the difference being sold here.

Both colourways are references to the company's own back catalogue rather than new ideas. All Black revisits the monochrome concept the house first showed in 2006. All Red draws on the red ceramic it introduced in 2018. Reworking a twenty-year-old concept in a new material is a cheaper proposition than a new case shape and it addresses an existing collector base directly, which is worth noting when reading the price.

On where $24,900 sits, one comparison needs a caveat before it is useful. The Federation of the Swiss Watch Industry reported, and this paper carried on 20 August, that July exports of watches with an export price above CHF 3,000 rose 12% by value inside a total up 9.6%. That threshold is an export price, not a retail one, and a watch retailing at $24,900 sits far above it on either measure, so the comparison is directional only. What it does establish is that the segment this watch is priced into was the growing part of July, not the flat part.

The desk's view: this is a materials story dressed as a launch, and materials stories are the ones that travel down the trade. If overmoulded texture holds up in wear, the technique reaches lower price points inside two or three seasons, because the process cost sits in tooling rather than in the material itself. For a retailer the near-term question is narrower and it is about the case: a $24,900 rubber watch asks a customer to accept a precious-metal price for a non-precious material, and that argument has to be made at the counter by a person, not by a press release.

title: 1,600 square feet at South Coast Plaza: Jessica McCormack takes the West Coast
dek: The London jeweller's second US store opened on 28 August at 3333 Bristol Street, Costa Mesa, in a Jewel Court that already holds Cartier, Chopard, Piaget and Harry Winston. Rodeo Drive follows in 2027.
body: Jessica McCormack opened a 1,600 square foot boutique at South Coast Plaza, 3333 Bristol Street in Costa Mesa, on 28 August. It is the London house's second store in the United States and its first on the West Coast. The first, on Madison Avenue in New York, opened in 2025. A third is planned for Rodeo Drive in Beverly Hills in 2027, so this is the middle step of a three-store American programme rather than a one-off.

The address is the substance of the story. South Coast Plaza's Jewel Court already holds Buccellati, Cartier, Chopard, Piaget, Harry Winston and David Yurman. A 1,600 square foot independent taking a unit in that corridor is buying proximity to the four largest maison names in American mall retail, and paying for footfall that has already been qualified by somebody else's marketing. It is the opposite of the street-level London model the house is known for and it is a deliberate choice.

Size is worth holding onto as a number rather than an impression. At 1,600 square feet the Costa Mesa store is a small format by the standards of the neighbours in that court, which is consistent with a house selling a narrow, recognisable signature rather than a broad catalogue. Small formats in high-rent corridors carry a specific risk and a specific advantage: revenue per square foot has to be high, but the absolute rent exposure stays containable if the corridor cools.

This desk has no revenue, unit-economics or lease figure for the store and none has been published, so none is estimated here. What can be said is the shape of the expansion: one store in 2025, a second in August 2026, a third announced for 2027, all three in the United States, and all three in addresses where the rent is a marketing line as much as a cost line.

The desk's view: the interesting thing about this opening is the corridor, not the jeweller. Independent houses have historically expanded in the US through wholesale accounts and trunk shows, which is cheap and slow and leaves the brand in somebody else's case. Taking a unit in a Jewel Court is expensive and fast and puts the brand in its own. Any independent watching this should note the sequence, because the Rodeo Drive announcement in 2027 will be the test of whether the model funded itself or was funded by the London business.

title: $4,366.10 gold and $1,753.00 platinum: the board is back at 19 August
dek: Gold fell 1.85% at press time, silver 3.13%, platinum 2.12% and palladium 3.84%. Three of the four now sit within 2.1% of their 19 August marks, and August's rally is gone.
body: All four metals on this paper's board fell in Tuesday's early session, and all four were re-read at press time and written back to the tape. Gold is $4,366.10 the ounce, down $82.19 or 1.8476% on Monday's close of $4,448.286. Silver is $64.44, down $2.08 or 3.1272%. Platinum is $1,753.00, down $37.92 or 2.1173%. Palladium is $1,304.00, down $52.11 or 3.8429%. The readings are Kitco's bid at 06:00 ET, checked against CNBC's quote pages at 06:02 ET. Compared like with like, midpoint to midpoint rather than bid to last, the two pages sit 0.0337% apart on gold, 0.1033% on silver, 0.0142% on platinum and 0.1499% on palladium. Palladium's own quoted spread was $40.00, or 3.067% of the bid, and CNBC's last sits on the midpoint of it. That is the trap this desk has been caught by before, and it is a wide quote rather than a disagreement. No outside-source divergence is disclosed this session, because there is none.

The comparison that matters is not with Monday. It is with 19 August. On this tape gold read $4,360.00 that morning and reads $4,366.10 now, $6.10 or 0.14% above it. Silver read $63.12 and reads $64.44, up 2.09%. Platinum read $1,726.00 and reads $1,753.00, up 1.56%. Thirteen days of trading have left the three metals a jeweller actually buys within 2.1% of where they started. Measured from the top instead, the highest gold mark this tape recorded in August was $4,643.90 on 24 August, and today's reading is $277.80 or 5.98% below it. Silver's highest was $70.37 on 28 August, 8.43% above today. Platinum's was $1,883.00 on the same morning, 6.90% above. Palladium's was $1,405.00 on 29 August, 7.19% above. Those are marks on this tape, read at the same hour each morning, and they are not intraday highs; outside reporting has gold trading as high as $4,697 on 25 August, which is a different measure and not a contradiction of ours.

The cause is not new and this desk will not dress it as new. Gold's worst session on our record, $150.10 in a day, ran on 29 August after the Federal Reserve chair's Jackson Hole remarks, and this paper printed it then. Reporting on 31 August has markets moving further toward pricing a rate rise at the September meeting. The published probabilities differ between outlets by more than twenty points, from about a third to about two thirds, so this desk prints the direction and withholds the number until one of them can be stood behind. What the board itself says needs no outside help. The gold-silver ratio is 67.75, from 66.46 on Monday. Silver fell harder than gold, which is what happens when the trade sells the whole complex rather than forms a view on any one metal.

For the trade the accounting runs in both directions, and this is the week it turns. This paper reported on 29 August that Chow Sang Sang's profit for the half to 30 June rose 139% on revenue up 17%, and said at the time that a margin doubled by the metal in the safe getting dearer is a business getting lucky rather than getting better. Eight days from the 24 August high, the same line runs backwards. A retailer holding gold inventory bought against an ounce at $4,643.90 is carrying it this morning against $4,366.10. Nothing about the shop has changed and nothing about demand has been measured; the balance sheet moves anyway. The jewellers who will find this quarter hardest are the ones whose last strong number came from the metal rather than from the counter.

The desk's view: a board that gives back thirteen days in eight is not a verdict on jewellery demand and should not be read as one. It is a verdict on rates, and the next scheduled thing that can move it is the September Federal Reserve meeting rather than anything happening in a shop. The number to hold onto is the 19 August comparison rather than the fall from the high, because the high is where the trade wishes it had sold and 19 August is where the market actually was before a fortnight of noise. Price your inventory off the second number. One further note, on ourselves: the gold beat's file this morning stood its sweep down under the heading Labor Day, US markets closed. Labor Day 2026 falls on Monday 7 September. Today is Tuesday 1 September, the markets were open, and this is the story that sweep would have found.

title: $687 a carat: lab-grown's one-dollar drift becomes a thirteen-dollar step
dek: CaratRadar's one-carat average fell $13 to $687 on 1 September, down 1.86% in a session. Every other move on this tape since 5 August was three dollars or less.
body: The one-carat lab-grown reference this paper carries fell to $687 on 1 September, from $700, a drop of $13 or 1.8571% in a single session. The figure is CaratRadar's average asking price for a one-carat lab-grown stone, read directly from the page by this desk, which carries its own dateline of 1 September and reports 1,204,718 active listings behind it. It is the lowest reading in this tape's record, and that record begins on 5 August 2026, so the claim is scoped to twenty-one sessions and no further. What makes it worth a page is not the level but the size of the step.

Until this morning the series had one shape and it was a drift. The mark peaked at $711 on 8 August and came down in ones and twos: $710, $707, $705, $704, $703, $701, $700. Across the whole of that run the largest single-day move was three dollars, on 14 August, which was 0.4225%. Today's move is $13, four and a third times the largest daily fall the series had previously produced, and it comes after two sessions at $700 in which nothing moved at all. Cumulatively the reference has lost $24, or 3.3755%, since the 8 August high. Most of that was accumulated a dollar at a time over three and a half weeks; more than half of the last week's loss arrived this morning.

The natural side is not moving with it, and the honest thing is to say that the two cannot be compared day to day. This paper's RapNet Diamond Index mark is a monthly figure and still carries its 24 July date, so there is no natural reading for 1 September to set against this one. The most recent natural data this desk can point to is Rapaport's Diamond Pulse newsletter published in early August, which reports July rather than August: one-carat prices staged a broad turnaround in July, reversing June's declines across nearly every category, with K-M VS stones moving from a 0.1% loss to a 2.8% gain, D-F SI declines narrowing to 0.2% from 2.1%, and G-J SI reversing to a 0.2% gain from a 0.3% decline. That is a month old and it is natural goods, not made ones. Set beside a lab-grown series that has not posted a single up day since this tape opened, it describes two markets that have stopped rhyming.

One caution for anyone pricing off this, because the trade routinely quotes three different numbers as though they were one. The $687 here is an average asking price for a finished one-carat stone in a retail-facing listings pool. The chip on this site's own tape reads $475, and that is a different thing again: the midpoint of the published CVD wholesale band for a one-carat D-F VS stone. This paper's lab-grown price list carries a third, $545 the carat as a retail ask. None of the three is wrong and none of them substitutes for another. A merchant reading a 1.86% fall in the listings average should not assume the same fall has reached the wholesale band, which moves on a slower clock and is republished rather than ticked.

The desk's view: a drift that becomes a step is usually a repricing rather than a trade, and the thing to watch this week is whether $687 holds or whether it was the first of several. The series has spent a month proving it can fall by a dollar without anyone noticing, which is precisely why a thirteen-dollar day is information. For retailers the practical consequence is narrow and immediate: lab-grown goods bought against a $700 average are carrying a 1.86% paper loss this morning, and unlike natural stones there is no scarcity argument that brings them back. The floor for a manufactured product is the cost of manufacturing it, and nothing in this series has yet found it.

title: RMB 3.641 billion, down 20.79%: Chow Tai Seng's margin rose anyway
dek: Revenue fell 20.79% and net profit 24.24% in the six months to 30 June. Gross margin rose 6.61 points to 36.95%, and second-quarter profit fell 54.2%.
body: Chow Tai Seng, listed in Shenzhen as 002867, reported revenue of RMB 3.641 billion for the six months to 30 June 2026, down 20.79% on the same half a year earlier, and net profit attributable to shareholders of RMB 450 million, down 24.24%. Stripping out exceptional items the profit was RMB 436 million, down 24.95%. Gross margin went the other way, rising 6.61 percentage points to 36.95% from 30.34%. The company proposed an interim distribution of RMB 174 million. The results were released on the evening of 25 August and are carried consistently by Sina Finance, Eastmoney and several other Chinese financial outlets; the company's own stated reason for the fall is that violent swings in the global gold price put jewellery consumption under pressure.

The margin line is the one worth sitting with, because it looks like good news and is not. A jewellery retailer's gross margin is a percentage of a smaller number, and gold rising does two things at once: it lifts the value of goods already on the shelf, which widens the margin, and it raises the shelf price to a customer who then buys less, which shrinks the revenue those margins are taken on. Chow Tai Seng shows both effects in one set of accounts. Applying the reported margin to the reported revenue, gross profit is roughly RMB 1.345 billion this half against roughly RMB 1.394 billion on the larger revenue base of a year ago. The percentage improved by 6.61 points and the money still went down. A margin that widens while volume falls is a price effect, not a trading achievement.

The half also hides a worse quarter. Second-quarter revenue was RMB 1.69 billion, down 12.3%, and second-quarter net profit was RMB 156 million, down 54.2%. That profit fall is more than twice the rate recorded across the full six months, which means the first quarter must have been considerably better than the second and that the deterioration is accelerating rather than levelling. It also means the headline pair of figures, minus 20.79% and minus 24.24%, understates where the business was by June. Anyone modelling the second half off the half-year numbers is starting from a base the company had already fallen below.

Set against the other Hong Kong and mainland name this paper covered days ago, the same six months produced opposite results from the same metal. Chow Sang Sang's half to 30 June, reported here on 29 August, took HK$12.88 billion of revenue, up 17%, and HK$2.15 billion of profit, up 139%. Chow Tai Seng's revenue fell a fifth and its profit a quarter over the identical window. Both companies name gold as the reason. The difference is where each sits relative to the metal: Chow Sang Sang's release credits improved retail sales together with an unrealised gain on the revaluation of its bullion lending, against an unrealised loss the year before, while Chow Tai Seng is describing a consumer who stopped buying at the new price. One company was long the metal on its balance sheet and one was selling it across a counter, and in a rising-gold half those are not the same business.

The desk's view: this is the clearest paired evidence yet that 2026's Chinese jewellery results are being written by the gold price rather than by the jewellery, and the trade should stop reading either number as a demand signal. The instructive figure is the second-quarter profit fall of 54.2%, because it is the one furthest from the metal and closest to the customer. It should also be read against this morning's board, where gold has given back everything it gained since 19 August. The revaluation that flattered one set of accounts is reversing, and the consumer who balked at the high price has not yet been given a reason to come back. The next set of Chinese interims will be the first in a while where the metal helps nobody.

title: $2,666.92 a polished carat, $82.66 a rough one: Antwerp's two books split
dek: Antwerp exported 1.15% fewer polished carats for 15.99% more dollars in the seven months to July, and 10.90% more rough carats for 17.73% fewer dollars. Per carat, polished rose 17.34% and rough fell 25.82%.
body: The Antwerp World Diamond Centre's July statistics workbook, last saved on 26 August and downloaded and read directly by this desk rather than through the summary page that sits above it, records two trades moving in opposite directions over the same seven months. Polished exports for January to July 2026 came to 1,581,439.42 carats worth $4,217,580,162, against 1,599,866.76 carats worth $3,636,115,968 in the same months of 2025. That is 18,427.34 fewer carats, a fall of 1.15%, carrying $581,464,194 more, a rise of 15.99%. Rough exports went the other way: 19,917,971.55 carats worth $1,646,417,080 against 17,960,158.83 carats worth $2,001,229,753, which is 1,957,812.72 more carats, up 10.90%, for $354,812,673 fewer dollars, down 17.73%.

Divide each side and the story stops being about volume. The average polished carat leaving Antwerp was worth $2,666.92 in the seven months to July, against $2,272.76 a year earlier, a rise of 17.34%. The average rough carat leaving was worth $82.66 against $111.43, a fall of 25.82%. In the first seven months of 2025 a polished carat out of Antwerp was worth 20.40 times a rough one. It is now worth 32.26 times as much. The spread between the two ends of this trade has widened by nearly twelve turns in a year.

The import side tells a jeweller where the value is added and where it is not. Antwerp took in 2,348,081.16 polished carats at $1,897.93 each and sent out 1,581,439.42 at $2,666.92 each. The carat that leaves is worth 40.52% more than the carat that arrives. That figure is a difference in mix rather than a trading margin, and it should be read as one: Antwerp is not marking up the same stones, it is importing a broader book and exporting a narrower, better one. On rough the same comparison inverts. Rough came in at $84.74 a carat and left at $82.66, so the average rough carat leaving Antwerp is worth 2.46% less than the average rough carat arriving.

One caveat belongs in the same breath as the headline, and the workbook supplies it. The July month on its own does not repeat the seven-month pattern at anything like the same strength. Polished exports in July 2026 were 228,701.17 carats for $499,154,341, or $2,182.56 a carat, against $2,112.43 in July 2025. That is a rise of 3.32%, not 17.34%. Rough exports in July ran $92.70 a carat against $116.05, a fall of 20.12%. The rough collapse is still there in the single month. The polished per-carat surge has largely gone out of it. Whatever pulled the polished average up did most of its work earlier in the year.

The desk's view: this is what a squeeze looks like from the middle of the pipeline rather than from either end of it. Antwerp is handling more rough for less money and less polished for more money, which is the arithmetic of a cutting centre being paid better for finished goods while the raw material it buys and passes on gets cheaper and more plentiful. That is a good year to be a trader of polished and a poor one to be a trader of rough, and the July column is a warning that the good half of it is already fading.

title: 76.9 million carats, 3.1% of the value: Dubai gives lab-grown its own desk
dek: DMCC has split lab-grown diamonds into a standalone vertical. The 2025 figures it published alongside show volume up 91.5% to 76.9 million carats and value up 7.5% to $1.3 billion. Those two rates are the story.
body: The Dubai Multi Commodities Centre announced on 30 August that it is establishing a standalone Lab-Grown Diamond Vertical, a separate trading and licensing platform for man-made stones rather than a line inside its existing diamond business. The figures published with the announcement cover calendar 2025: 76.9 million carats traded, up 91.5% year on year, at a value of $1.3 billion, up 7.5%. DMCC also puts the rise since 2022 at 109%, from 36.8 million carats, and sizes the global sector at about $30 billion.

The two growth rates do not sit comfortably together, and the gap between them is the number worth carrying. If volume rose 91.5% and value rose 7.5%, the implied 2024 base is 40.16 million carats worth about $1.209 billion, or $30.11 a carat. The 2025 figure is $16.91 a carat. On DMCC's own two percentages, the average price of a lab-grown carat moving through Dubai fell 43.86% in a single year. Ahmed Bin Sulayem, DMCC's executive chairman and chief executive, said lab-grown diamonds have reached the point where "they need dedicated market infrastructure". The price series underneath is what that infrastructure will have to be built on.

Set the lab-grown line against the whole Dubai book and the proportions come into focus. This paper reported on 15 July, from DMCC's own 2025 ledger, that the emirate's total diamond trade reached $41.7 billion on 359.5 million carats. Lab-grown is therefore 21.39% of the carats Dubai handled last year and 3.12% of the dollars. Put another way, the average carat crossing Dubai was worth $115.99 and the average lab-grown carat was worth $16.91, about one-seventh as much. A fifth of the volume is generating a thirty-second of the value.

For a trading hub that is an argument for separation rather than against it. Goods that move in these volumes at these prices need different licensing, different storage economics and different settlement from stones worth a hundred times more per carat, and mixing them inside one set of statistics makes both harder to read. The commercial risk sits elsewhere: a vertical is a fixed piece of infrastructure and the price line running through it has fallen by more than two fifths in a year on the operator's own arithmetic. Dubai is building a permanent room for a trade whose unit economics are still moving fast.

The desk's view: the announcement will be read in the trade as Dubai blessing lab-grown, and that is the smaller half of it. The larger half is that DMCC has now published, in two percentages twelve points apart, the clearest public statement anyone has made this year of what is actually happening to lab-grown prices at wholesale. Volume nearly doubled and value barely moved. Any retailer still setting lab-grown margins off a 2024 cost sheet should read those two numbers together and then read their own.

title: A$2.1m to A$10m: the line Michael Hill's July update left out
dek: The audited full year gives the profit figure the trading update did not. Net profit rose from A$2.1 million to A$10.0 million, and net debt fell from A$41.9 million to A$5.5 million, on group sales of A$654.7 million.
body: Michael Hill has published the audited result for the 52 weeks to 28 June 2026, and it carries the number its July trading update did not. Net profit came to A$10.0 million against A$2.1 million a year earlier, which is 4.76 times the prior figure. Net debt at the balance date was A$5.5 million against A$41.9 million in 2025, a reduction of A$36.4 million or 86.87%. Group sales were A$654.7 million, up 2.04% on FY25's A$641.6 million, with group same-store sales up 3.0%, Australia up 4.8%, Canada up 7.0% and New Zealand up 3.6%.

This desk reported the sales side on 3 August and closed that piece with an explicit test: judge it again when the profit line lands, because 2% of revenue growth against a metal that rose for most of the year is compatible with several very different margin outcomes. The line has landed and the answer is the favourable one. Net margin went from 0.33% of sales to 1.53%. That is still a thin margin by any standard, and it is roughly four and a half times thinner than it looks in the growth rate, which is the ordinary arithmetic of quadrupling a very small number.

One figure needs disclosing rather than smoothing over. Rapaport's report of the result gives group revenue as A$655.7 million. The company's own release, and the several independent accounts of it this desk checked, give A$654.7 million against a prior year of A$641.6 million. This paper printed A$654.7 million on 3 August and prints it again today, because that is the figure the company published and it reconciles with the stated 2.0% growth rate. Readers should treat the higher number as an outside-source divergence, not as a revision.

The store maths reconciles cleanly with what was reported in July and is worth restating because it is the strategy. The network finished at 281 shops, 157 in Australia, 81 in Canada and 43 in New Zealand, down from 287 after eight closures and two openings, with four of those openings and closings reshaped into flagship formats across Australia and Canada. Chief executive Jonathan Waecker said the company had "simplified the business, and we've doubled down on quality jewelry". Rob Fyfe retires as chair at the end of November after five years in the seat and twelve on the board, with deputy chair Claudia Batten named to succeed him.

The desk's view: the debt line is the one to keep. A mid-market chain that took A$36.4 million of net debt off its balance sheet in a year while closing a net six doors and lifting same-store sales 3% has bought itself the thing that mid-market jewellery chains almost never have, which is the ability to sit out a bad Christmas. The profit multiple will be quoted everywhere and it is the least informative number in the release. A$5.5 million of net debt is the one that changes what this company can do next year.

title: $4.3 million, priced in 2015: the only number on the Vienna necklace is a decade old
dek: A 1939 Van Cleef & Arpels necklace of more than 200 carats was taken from Vienna's MAK museum on Thursday. Every published valuation traces to one Sotheby's sale in December 2015, ten years and eight months ago.
body: Two men took a Van Cleef & Arpels diamond necklace from the MAK, Vienna's Museum of Applied Arts beside the Stadtpark, on Thursday 29 August, and an Austrian manhunt is under way. The piece dates from 1939 and carries more than 200 carats across more than 600 round and baguette-cut diamonds, in a graduated line supporting a flexible bib sunburst centred on an articulated round stone of roughly six carats. It was made for Queen Nazli of Egypt and later passed to her daughter Fawzia, who married Mohammad Reza Pahlavi.

The valuation being reported everywhere is $4.3 million, and it should be read for what it is. That figure is the price the necklace made at Sotheby's in New York in December 2015. It is not an insurance value, not a current appraisal and not a 2026 estimate. It is a single auction result that is ten years and eight months old, and this desk could find no more recent published price on the piece. A museum theft is one of the few events in this trade where a number gets repeated in hundreds of outlets within a day without anyone asking when it was struck.

The internal arithmetic is more durable than the headline figure and more useful to anyone who may be offered the goods. More than 200 carats across more than 600 stones puts the average stone below 0.334 carats. On the 2015 price, the necklace made about $21,500 a carat. Those are the proportions of a piece whose value sits in design, provenance and assembly rather than in any individual stone. Broken up, the constituent parts are small goods in a market where small goods are cheap, which is precisely the calculation a thief has to get wrong for the theft to be worth doing.

It is the third significant raid on a European collection this desk has recorded in recent months, after the Musee Lalique theft in July, put at 4.5 million euros or about $5.1 million, and the Louvre job at $102 million. What links them is not method but target selection: cultural institutions holding named, photographed, unsellable pieces. The Vienna necklace cannot be sold as itself to any legitimate buyer anywhere, and its recovery odds rest on whether it is still assembled.

Correction, 1 September 2026. This article first gave the Musee Lalique theft of July 2026 as 4 million euros, or about $4.6 million. The correct figure is 4.5 million euros, or about $5.1 million. The lower number was the first estimate, carried by National Jeweler on 7 July from a source close to the investigation, when about 20 pieces were thought to have gone. National Jeweler revised it the next day, once the inventory was complete, to 27 pieces worth an estimated 4.5 million euros, or about $5.1 million, and Smithsonian Magazine put the loss at roughly $5 million on 10 July. What was correct as published: this paper's own report of 14 July carried the revised 4.5 million euro figure and remains right. The fault was in reaching back past it to the superseded first estimate. The Louvre figure in the same sentence was true but uncited when this ran, and is now sourced: 88 million euros, or $102 million, given by the Paris prosecutor Laure Beccuau on 21 October 2025. Nothing else in this article changes, including the $4.3 million Sotheby's result of December 2015.

The desk's view: the clock on this one is measured in days, not months, because the only version of the necklace worth $4.3 million is the intact version, and the only version that is easy to move is the broken one. For jewellers reading it as a security story, note the specific lesson the number teaches rather than the drama: an item whose last public valuation is a decade old is an item nobody has properly repriced, and that is as true of the safe in the back room as it is of a museum case in Vienna.

title: 392 districts, 26 of 36 states: where India's hallmark law now reaches
dek: The Third Amendment Order, issued 3 August, adds 12 districts to mandatory gold hallmarking, taking the count from 380 to 392 across 26 states and union territories. This paper had not carried it. It is 28 days old.
body: India's Ministry of Consumer Affairs, Food and Public Distribution issued the Hallmarking of Gold Jewellery and Gold Artefacts (Third Amendment) Order, 2026 on 3 August, on the advice of the Bureau of Indian Standards and under the Bureau of Indian Standards Act, 2016. It adds twelve districts to the mandatory hallmarking regime, taking the total from 380 to 392. The twelve are Kokrajhar and Lakhimpur in Assam, Panipat in Haryana, Bhind, Khandwa and Vidisha in Madhya Pradesh, Bhandara in Maharashtra, Angul in Odisha, Kotputli-Behror in Rajasthan, Kancheepuram in Tamil Nadu, Udham Singh Nagar in Uttarakhand and Jhargram in West Bengal.

This item is being carried here for a reason that should be stated rather than disguised. It is 28 days old. It was reported in the Indian trade and financial press on 10 and 11 August and this paper did not carry it, and nothing about it is new today. It is printed because it is a rule in force that binds jewellers in twelve named districts and because a paper's archive is only useful if the live regulations are actually in it. It is not printed as news, and it will not be run again.

The coverage arithmetic is the part that has not been published clearly anywhere this desk could find. The revised annexure covers 392 districts across 26 states and union territories. India has 36 states and union territories in total, so the regime now reaches 72.22% of them by that count. The district-level denominator is less useful than it looks: published totals for the number of districts in India currently range from 784 to about 802 depending on the source and the date, because states create and redraw districts continuously, and this desk will not print a percentage built on a denominator it cannot pin down. States and union territories is the firm measure, and 26 of 36 is the firm figure.

The mechanism matters more than the map for anyone trading into these districts. Mandatory hallmarking means a jeweller in a covered district may not sell gold jewellery or artefacts without a BIS hallmark carrying the six-digit alphanumeric HUID, and registration with BIS is the precondition for doing so. The order is the third amendment of 2026, following one on 28 April, to a parent order that dates from 15 January 2020. The pattern is a steady district-by-district widening rather than a national switch-on, which means the compliance question for a multi-state retailer is not whether the rule applies but in which of its shops it applies this month.

The desk's view: the twelve names are the whole content of this order and most coverage of it led with the number 392 instead. A jeweller in Panipat or Angul or Kancheepuram has a registration to complete and a stock of unhallmarked pieces to deal with, and a jeweller three districts over has neither. Read the list, not the total. This paper should have carried it on 10 August and did not, which is why it appears at the bottom of today's edition rather than anywhere near the top.

title: Palladium fell 2.21%, and the spread you would pay to trade it was 2.91%
dek: The week reopened with silver the only one of four metals in the green. Gold $4,444.80, silver $66.879, platinum $1,797.00, palladium $1,374.00, all re-read at press time and written back to the tape.
body: All four precious metals were re-read at press time this morning and all four had moved off the tape's opening mark, so all four are written back and print here as the paper's marks of record. Gold is $4,444.80 the ounce, down $9.60 or 0.2155% on Friday's close of $4,454.40. Silver is $66.879, up $0.626 or 0.9449%. Platinum is $1,797.00, down $22.00 or 1.2095%. Palladium is $1,374.00, down $31.00 or 2.2064%. Silver is the only one of the four in the green, and palladium is much the worst of the board.

The figure worth stopping on is not palladium's fall but what it costs to act on it. Kitco quoted palladium at press time at $1,374.00 bid against $1,414.00 asked, a spread of $40.00. That is 2.9112% of the bid. Palladium's entire move on the day was 2.2064%. The cost of crossing the quote was wider than the thing being quoted moved, which is a plain description of a market too thin to trade in size. Gold's spread was $2.00 on $4,444.80, or 0.0450%. Silver's was $0.25, or 0.3738%. Platinum's was $10.00, or 0.5565%.

That spread also explains a disclosure this paper made yesterday and is now correcting the reading of. The tape reported TradingEconomics at $1,426.00 on palladium as a 1.207% divergence from Kitco. Kitco's ask at the same moment was $1,429.00. TradingEconomics was quoting inside Kitco's own bid and ask, not away from the market, and the apparent divergence was an artefact of comparing another venue's mid against one side of a $40 spread. Today all four metals were checked mid to mid against CNBC, and all four agreed inside 0.08%: gold 0.0286%, silver 0.0800%, platinum 0.0455%, palladium 0.0359%. No outside-source divergence is disclosed this session.

For the bench the relevant ratio moved in the direction that helps. Gold bought 66.46 ounces of silver at these marks against 67.23 on Friday, so silver gained just under eight tenths of a point on gold in one session. Platinum sits 59.57% below gold, which is the discount that has been driving substitution enquiries in white metal all year. Gold at $4,444.80 is $1,429.04 per ten grams, which matters in India this week, where the customs tariff value for gold stands at $1,500 per ten grams and now exceeds the metal by $70.96, or 4.9656%, a wider gap than the $67.88 this paper printed on Saturday.

The desk's view: a 2.21% fall in palladium is not a signal when the spread around it is 2.91%, and anyone reading that number as a market view rather than as noise is reading a quote convention. The honest summary of the session is narrower and duller: silver up a point, gold flat, the two white metals soft, and one of them barely trading. The number in this piece with real consequences attached is the last one, which is the Indian tariff gap, because that one is settled by a notification rather than by a market and it has widened again.

title: $1,500 for ten grams: India's customs base outruns the metal
dek: Notification 71/2026 set the tariff value for imported gold at US$1,500 per 10 grams on 25 August. At Friday's close 10 grams is worth $1,432.12. The gap is 4.7396%, and duty is charged on the larger number.
body: India's customs service has fixed the value of imported gold at US$1,500 per 10 grams. Notification No. 71/2026-Customs (N.T.), signed on 25 August and effective from 26 August, raises the figure from $1,407, the level set eleven days earlier by Notification No. 70/2026. That is $93 more, a rise of 6.6098%. Silver was left alone at $2,097 the kilogram, and so were palm oil, soybean oil, brass scrap and areca nuts at $11,574 the tonne. Gold was the only line in the table that moved.

A tariff value is not a price. It is the base Indian customs applies for ad valorem duty whatever an importer actually paid, and it is reset roughly twice a month. The point of the exercise is to track the world market closely enough that the base is neither a gift nor a penalty. This one no longer does. At $1,500 per 10 grams the notification implies gold at $4,665.52 the ounce. This desk re-read Kitco at press time this morning and gold is $4,454.40, the same figure the tape has carried since Friday's close and unchanged because spot has not traded since. Ten grams of gold is worth $1,432.12.

The gap is $67.88, or 4.7396% above what the metal is worth, and it was not opened by anyone's error. On 25 August, the day the notification was signed, this paper's mark of record was $4,634.20, which puts 10 grams at $1,489.93. The base stood $10.07 clear of the metal even then, 0.6759%. What widened it was Friday. Gold fell $150.10 in one session, the worst day this tape has recorded in twenty-three sessions, and a fortnightly notification does not move on a Friday.

The cost of that is arithmetic. The combined effective import duty on gold bullion has been 15% since 13 May, when Notification No. 15/2026-Customs took basic customs duty to 10% and the surcharge and cess carried the rest. Fifteen percent of $1,500 is $225.00 per 10 grams. Fifteen percent of $1,432.12 is $214.82. The difference of $10.18 per 10 grams is $1,018.16 on every kilogram landed while both numbers stand. An importer clearing a hundred kilograms this week pays about $101,816 of duty on gold that is not in the box.

The desk's view: nobody has done anything wrong here and this is not a scandal. A base reset twice a month cannot chase a 3.26% one-day fall, and the next notification will most likely bring it back down. But the trade should know which way the error runs and what it costs, because it runs one way at a time and nobody publishes the gap. An importer who ships in the last days of a fortnight after a hard fall pays for the calendar; one who ships after a rally is paid by it. The number worth watching is not the duty rate, which has not changed since May. It is the distance between the base and the metal, and this morning that distance is 4.7396%.

title: Two counters, one Friday: Dubai adds 2%, Chow Tai Fook adds 40%
dek: Dubai's published 24-carat rate of 536.75 dirhams a gram is 2.05% over the world price. Chow Tai Fook's Chinese counter at 1,348 yuan is 39.84% over. They are not the same kind of price.
body: Friday's selloff reached the retail counter over the weekend, and it reached two of them at very different heights. Chow Tai Fook's mainland China counter price for 999 fine gold read 1,348.00 yuan the gram when this desk fetched it at press time today, flat against yesterday on the page's own reading and down 39 yuan from the 1,387 this paper carried on 28 August, a fall of 2.8118%. In Dubai, Emarat Al Youm published a 24-carat retail rate of 536.75 dirhams the gram, bylined 11:56 on 29 August, alongside 497 for 22-carat, 476.75 for 21-carat and 408.50 for 18-carat.

Both are quoted in local currency against a metal that trades in dollars, so the comparison has to be made in dollars. The dirham is pegged at 3.6725 to the dollar, and the yuan read 6.73084 on xe.com at 04:12 UTC this morning. That puts Dubai's 24-carat rate at $146.1538 the gram and Chow Tai Fook's counter at $200.2722. Gold itself, at the $4,454.40 this desk re-read on Kitco this morning, is $143.2123 the gram.

Dubai's published rate is 2.0540% over the metal. Chow Tai Fook's is 39.8429% over. Per gram that is a difference of $54.12, and the Chinese counter is 1.3703 times the Gulf one for the same weight at effectively the same purity.

The spread is not evidence of anything improper, and a reader who treats it as one has misread what the two numbers are. Dubai's published gold rate is a metal rate: the souk quotes bullion and charges making separately, which is why the 22, 21 and 18-carat lines beneath it divide down almost exactly by purity. Chow Tai Fook's is a finished-jewellery counter price with craftsmanship, brand and margin already inside it, which is the ordinary shape of Chinese branded gold retail. They are not the same kind of price and they never were. What they share is the word gold and the fact that a consumer in either city reads them as the price of it.

The desk's view: the lesson is not that Chinese gold is dear. It is that the phrase gold price does not survive a border. A shopper weighing 536.75 in Dubai against 1,348 in Shenzhen, or either against the $4,454.40 on a screen, is comparing three different products: bullion, a metal rate quoted before making, and a finished object. This paper prints one price per metal per morning precisely because the alternative is this. Anyone quoting a counter figure as the price of gold should say which of the three they mean. The honest reading of Friday is that the world price fell 3.2604%, Chow Tai Fook's counter followed it down 2.8118%, and this paper holds no prior Dubai figure to measure the Gulf move against and will not invent one.

title: Pigeon blood, issued in Jaipur: GSI brings the trade names home
dek: GSI now issues Pigeon Blood, Royal Blue and Padparadscha reports from Jaipur, Mumbai, New York and Bangkok. Untreated stones only. Jaipur cuts the world's finest rubies and could not name them at home.
body: A ruby cut in Jaipur can now be called pigeon blood in Jaipur. Gemological Science International has begun issuing coloured stone reports carrying the recognised colour trade names, Rapaport reported on 19 August: Pigeon Blood for ruby, Royal Blue and Padparadscha for sapphire. The reports are available from the laboratory's Jaipur, Mumbai, New York and Bangkok operations. It is the first time such reports have been issued in India.

The names are much older than the reports. Pigeon blood and royal blue have been trade language for generations and laboratory language since the 1990s, and they carry real money: a stone that qualifies sells at a premium to one that does not, on a judgement about colour that a buyer cannot make from a photograph. Until now a stone finished in Jaipur had to travel to a laboratory abroad to be given one. Meenu Brijesh Vyas, GSI's global head gemologist, said of the change: That ends today.

The criteria behind the names are not impressionistic. GSI defines each by specified ranges of hue, tone and saturation, assessed under standardised lighting and supported by spectroscopic and colorimetric analysis, and grants the designations only to untreated stones. Heated, diffused or otherwise enhanced material is not eligible whatever its colour. That last condition does most of the work, because heat is the commonest treatment in both ruby and sapphire and much the cheapest route to a colour that looks like the name.

The conditions sit close to what the Swiss laboratories already publish. SSEF requires of pigeon blood red a strong, vivid red saturation with no or only slight purplish tint, strong ultraviolet fluorescence from high chromium and low iron, no colour zoning seen from above, freedom from eye-visible dark inclusions and no fissure or cavity filling. Its royal blue requires strong, vivid blue without greenish, greyish or purple tint, a spectrum dominated by iron-titanium charge transfer, colour homogeneity and good transparency. SSEF applies pigeon blood red only to rubies showing no indication of any treatment. Another laboratory issuing on comparable terms in the city that cuts the stones changes where the judgement happens, not what the judgement is.

The desk's view: this is a logistics story wearing the clothes of a nomenclature story. The gemmology has not moved. What has moved is that the report can be written where the stone is finished, which takes weeks and a courier run out of the process and puts the premium-setting judgement inside the Indian trade rather than at the end of it. That is worth money in Jaipur. It is also worth watching for the obvious reason: a name that pays a premium is a name under pressure, and one more issuer is more supply of the name than there was before. The check on that is the untreated-only condition, and it is the line this paper will hold GSI to.

title: 875 fakes, $3.7 million: one parcel bound for a Georgia house
dek: US customs took 875 counterfeit pieces and five handbags at Indianapolis, carrying Cartier, Tiffany and Van Cleef marks. Retail value if genuine, $3.7 million. That is $4,228.57 a piece.
body: United States Customs and Border Protection took 875 counterfeit pieces of jewellery and five designer handbags out of a single parcel at the Indianapolis express consignment facility. The shipment came from Hong Kong and was addressed to a residence in Georgia. Had the jewellery been genuine, National Jeweler and Rapaport both put its retail value at $3.7 million. Across 875 pieces that is an average of $4,228.57 apiece.

The marks on the goods were the ones that always appear. National Jeweler lists Louis Vuitton, Chanel, Versace, Gucci, Tiffany and Co., Cartier and Van Cleef and Arpels; Rapaport's account of the same seizure names Cartier, Tiffany and Van Cleef and Arpels. The pieces were earrings, necklaces and bracelets. Brett Mueller, the Indianapolis port director, credited officers and import specialists working alongside brand owners rather than any single tip.

The $3.7 million is a suggested retail figure and deserves to be read as one. It is what the parcel would have been worth if every piece were real and sold at list, which is not what a counterfeit parcel is worth to anyone, including whoever ordered it. The figure customs publishes is the loss to the brands at full price, not the price paid in Hong Kong. It is the right number for measuring what was infringed and the wrong number for measuring what was smuggled, and the two get quoted interchangeably.

The destination is the part a retailer should read twice. This was not a container into a warehouse or a pallet into a wholesaler. It was a parcel to a house, in the volume a small seller carries, moving through a facility that exists to shift exactly that kind of package quickly. Eight hundred and seventy-five pieces is not personal use. It is inventory, and the channel it was travelling in is the one legitimate online sellers use.

The desk's view: the enforcement figure that matters to an independent jeweller is not $3.7 million, it is 875. A parcel that size going to a residential address is a small business being stocked, and it will compete on the same marketplaces as the shop down the road, at prices the shop cannot meet, quite possibly using photographs taken from the shop's own website. Customs caught this one because an officer pulled the package, and there is no reason to think the rate of pulling is high. The trade's defence was never the border, which sees a fraction of what crosses it. It is the authentication layer the resale platforms have built, and this paper has already priced how well that works: one marketplace turns away 38% of the Rolexes it is offered.

title: Gold lost $150.10 and silver 5.85%: the worst session this tape has recorded
dek: Friday's close puts gold at $4,454.40 and silver at $66.253, down 3.26% and 5.85% on Thursday's marks. Both are the largest one-day falls in the 23 sessions this tape has run. Palladium rose 1.74%.
body: This desk re-read all four metals on Kitco at press time this morning and wrote nothing back, because nothing had moved. Gold reads $4,454.40 the ounce, silver $66.253, platinum $1,819.00 and palladium $1,405.00, each identical to the 05:00 mark the tape desk filed. Today is Saturday, spot metal does not trade until Sunday evening, and Kitco's board carries an internal timestamp of 13:00 New York time on Friday across all four. These are Friday's last prints, read live today and confirmed unchanged, not a new session. The marks they replace are Thursday's: gold $4,604.50, silver $70.37, platinum $1,883.00 and palladium $1,381.00.

Measured against those, gold fell $150.10, or 3.2604%, and silver $4.117, or 5.8507%. This paper's tape has carried a daily mark of record for all four metals since 5 August, twenty-three sessions, and neither fall has a close rival in that record. The next-worst gold session on the tape is 27 August at 0.9259%, so Friday is 3.52 times worse than anything before it. The next-worst silver session is 19 August at 2.89%, and Friday is 2.02 times that. Silver set the tape's high-water mark of $70.37 on Thursday and gave 5.85% of it back on Friday, which is a record and its reversal on consecutive days. Gold's own high-water mark, $4,643.90 on 24 August, now sits $189.50 or 4.2542% above where the metal stopped.

The cause was named in Wyoming and is not in dispute. Federal Reserve chair Kevin Warsh used his first Jackson Hole keynote on Friday to say that better summer readings on the PCE and CPI indices did not tell him underlying inflation had improved. "Otherwise, we have work to do." He said more than half of the items tracked in the PCE have risen above 3% over the past year, against 32% in the twenty years before the pandemic and a post-pandemic peak of 77%. The market read a rate rise back into September: CME Group's FedWatch tool moved from about 35.5% the day before to 57.5% after the speech, on the Motley Fool's reading of it. Gold pays no interest, and a metal that pays no interest is repriced by the expectation of a higher one. An outside report earlier that morning had gold steady near $4,650 and December futures opening at $4,656.

The width of the day is the part a bench should carry. On Kitco's own board Friday's range ran $4,444.80 to $4,629.10, which is $184.30, or 4.146% of the low, and the metal finished $9.60 above the bottom of it and $174.70 below the top. Silver ran $65.998 to $71.230, a range of 7.928% of the low, and stopped 25.5 cents off the bottom. Palladium is the exception in every direction: up $24.00 or 1.7378% on the day, in a range of $1,304.00 to $1,492.00, and carrying a $40.00 bid-ask spread that is 2.847% of its own bid against gold's 0.0449%, sixty-three times wider. One outside divergence is disclosed. On platinum, TradingEconomics read $1,833.60 against Kitco's mid of $1,824.00, a gap of 0.526%, while CNBC at $1,820.15 agreed with Kitco; the tape is written at Kitco's bid on the two pages that agree, and the odd reading is printed here rather than dropped.

Correction, 30 August 2026. An earlier version of this article, and the matching entry in the record, put the distance between gold's high-water mark of $4,643.90 on 24 August and Friday's close at $189.50 or 4.0806% above where the metal stopped. The dollar figure was right and is unchanged. The percentage was not. 4.0806% is $189.50 divided by the high-water mark itself, which measures how far below its high the metal now sits, not how far above the metal the high sits. Measured as this sentence states it, against where the metal stopped, the figure is $189.50 divided by $4,454.40, or 4.2542%, and that is what now prints. The bad figure came from this desk's own arithmetic, not from a source. Both prices, the $189.50 gap, and every other percentage in this article were correct as published.

The desk's view: a jeweller does not need a view on the Federal Reserve to be hurt by this, and that is the whole problem with treating bullion as a market rather than a raw material. A counter that quoted a customer on Thursday afternoon and settled the metal on Friday afternoon lost 3.26% of the gold and 5.85% of the silver in between, on nobody's mistake. The gold-to-silver ratio moved from 65.43 to 67.23 in one session, 2.75% wider, which changes the economics of every mixed-metal piece on the bench. The practical instruction is unglamorous and it is the same one this desk gave when the metal was running the other way in the third week of August: quote with a metal clause or quote for an hour, because a workshop that prices a commission on Thursday and buys the gold on Monday is running a position it was never paid to run.
