title: OFAC moves the grandfathered deadline a year, to 1 September 2027
dek: General License No. 104B extends by one year the window for Russian-origin diamonds bought before sanctions. Stones over a carat must have left Russia before 1 March 2024; half to one carat before 1 September 2024.
body: The United States Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control issued General License No. 104B on 27 August, moving to 1 September 2027 a deadline that had stood at 1 September 2026. The licence covers loose, nonindustrial Russian-origin diamonds that were bought before the sanctions took effect and that had not entered the American market by the cutoffs the licence names. Stones of one carat and above must have left Russia before 1 March 2024. Stones between half a carat and one carat must have left before 1 September 2024. General License No. 103, which governs imports of diamond jewellery, is unchanged. This desk could not extract the licence text from OFAC's own recent-actions listing, which renders its results dynamically and returned no diamond entry to a plain fetch, and carries the detail from Rapaport's report of the release, which the bureau independently confirmed against the page's own publication metadata.

The arithmetic of a grandfathering clause is the arithmetic of how long goods can sit. A one-carat stone that qualifies under this licence left Russia before 1 March 2024, so by the new deadline it will have been outside Russia for at least 1,279 days, three and a half years. A half-carat stone left before 1 September 2024 and will have been out at least 1,095 days, three years to the day. The extension itself is 365 days. What has been extended, in other words, is not a trading window on new goods but the shelf life of a specific and closed population of stones that was already fixed in size on two dates in 2024 and has been shrinking ever since, as parcels clear or are written down.

Nobody has published how many carats are in that population, and the absence is the story's limit. Neither the licence as reported nor any trade body this desk reached puts a weight, a value or a count on the goods still waiting. Without it, a one-year extension cannot be priced. It can be read directionally: an authority that thought the remaining volume was trivial would let the deadline pass, and an authority that thought the market could absorb it at once would not have extended it three times. The instrument's own history is the only quantity available. A licence numbered 104B is the second amendment to a licence, and each amendment has bought the same population more time rather than releasing it.

There is a second reading, and it is about where those stones are rather than when they may move. A parcel grandfathered under 104B is legal in the United States and, under the Group of Seven's separate traceability regime, is documented as pre-sanction goods rather than as ordinary rough. That documentation follows the stone, and it is expensive to maintain across three and a half years of storage, insurance and financing on inventory nobody has sold. This desk has reported through August on the cost of holding rough that cannot be moved, and on Antwerp's July imports falling to 1,590,026 carats, the thinnest month in the fifty-five that its own body publishes. A pipeline that thin is a pipeline in which parked goods are a larger share of everything.

The desk's view: an extension is being read in parts of the trade as a softening, and it is closer to the opposite. Nothing in 104B lets a single new Russian stone in. It lets a fixed and ageing pile of stones that were already bought, already shipped and already documented stay eligible for another year, and it does so for the third time. If those goods were saleable at a price the holders would accept, three years and six months is long enough for them to have gone. A dealer looking at this notice should read it as the regulator confirming the overhang still exists, on the regulator's own evidence, rather than as a door opening. The stones are not stuck because of the deadline. The deadline exists because the stones are stuck.

title: A fourth source for Paraíba: GIA and Gübelin both put Ethiopia on the map
dek: Two laboratories said on 27 August that Ethiopian copper-bearing tourmaline meets the Paraíba definition. Gübelin first saw the material in May, GIA in June, and GIA studied a parcel of more than 100 rough and faceted stones.
body: The Gemological Institute of America and the Gübelin Gem Lab announced jointly on 27 August that Ethiopia is a new source of copper-bearing tourmaline meeting the widely accepted definition of Paraíba tourmaline. Until this week that definition had three producing countries behind it: Brazil, where the material was found in the 1980s, and Nigeria and Mozambique, which followed. Ethiopia is the fourth. The two laboratories reached the conclusion independently and on separate material. Gübelin first encountered stones with an unfamiliar chemical signature in early May. GIA began examining goods represented as Ethiopian in June and later received a parcel of more than one hundred rough and faceted samples for study. Both describe elevated concentrations of vanadium, lead and gallium as the separating markers, and neither has yet published the thresholds; the detailed findings are going to Gems & Gemology.

What makes this more than a locality note is what the same trade was told three months ago. In June the Swiss Gemmological Institute SSEF reported credible accounts of an Ethiopian deposit and said its own preliminary trace-element work on submitted stones showed considerable overlap with material from previously known localities, particularly Brazil. SSEF called origin determination on some of those specimens difficult and in some cases inconclusive, and said research was continuing to refine the methods needed to tell the material apart. Two laboratories have now done that work on their own samples and got an answer. The June position and the August position are not a contradiction; they are the ordinary distance between a first look and a characterised reference set, which in this case took roughly three months.

Origin is not a curiosity in this stone, it is most of the price. This paper reported on 30 July, from Rapaport's January survey of the trade, that Mozambican Paraíba had moved from around $7,000 a carat to between $10,000 and $12,000, and Brazilian material has always carried a multiple of the African price for the same colour. A fourth source enters that structure at an unknown place on it. Nobody has published a price for an Ethiopian stone, no parcel value or carat weight has been made public, and the colours described run wide: blue to bluish green, violet, purple and colourless, many showing colour zoning and compositional variation within a single stone. A material that varies that much inside itself does not price as one thing.

The practical consequence lands on the laboratory report rather than on the mine. Every serious Paraíba trades on an origin call, and until this week a report reading Brazil, Nigeria or Mozambique exhausted the options. Two laboratories now say the chemistry separates Ethiopian material by vanadium, lead and gallium, and both describe those as measurable rather than exotic determinations. That is the difference between a discovery that unsettles the trade and one it can absorb: an origin that can be read on ordinary laboratory equipment does not create a permanent doubt over stones already certified. What it does create is a window, between the announcement and the reference data being published, in which no dealer can be certain which country a stone bought last year came from.

The desk's view: the useful thing here is not that Ethiopia has Paraíba, it is that two competing laboratories announced it together and neither claimed to have got there first. Origin determination is a commercial product, sold in competition, and the ordinary incentive is to publish alone and early. A joint statement, made on independent samples, with the underlying data going to a peer-reviewed journal rather than a press release, is the behaviour a trade should want from the institutions that price its stones. For a dealer the near-term instruction is narrow and dull. Do not pay a Brazilian premium on an unreported stone bought this year, do not assume an existing certificate is wrong, and wait for the Gems and Gemology paper before repricing anything. For this desk, the note is that its longest-running gap closed on a story about method rather than about money.

title: Profit up 139% on revenue up 17%, and 47 shops closed
dek: Chow Sang Sang's half to 30 June took HK$12.88 billion, up 17%, and HK$2.15 billion of profit, up 139%. Same-store sales rose 38% in Hong Kong and Macau and 11% on the mainland.
body: Chow Sang Sang reported on 27 August that revenue for the six months to 30 June 2026 was HK$12.88 billion, about $1.64 billion, up 17% on the same half a year earlier. Retail sales were HK$12.71 billion, or $1.62 billion, up 18%, which is 98.68% of the whole group figure. Profit was HK$2.15 billion, about $274.6 million, up 139%. Same-store sales grew 11% in mainland China, made of 7% in the first quarter and 17% in the second, and 38% in Hong Kong and Macau, made of 46% and then 30%. The group closed a net 47 shops, predominantly on the mainland. The company said that key collections, including Cultural Blessings and Noir, recorded strong growth.

The gap between the two headline percentages is the result. Revenue rose 17% and profit rose 139%, which means the margin did most of the work rather than the sales. Working back from the company's own figures, the comparable half produced roughly HK$11.01 billion of revenue and about HK$900 million of profit, a net margin near 8.17%. This half returns 16.69% on the same measure. The margin has roughly doubled in twelve months at a chain whose shop count fell. That is what a gold-led half looks like at a retailer holding metal inventory into a rising price: the goods on the shelf appreciate faster than the cost of running the shelf, and every point of that lands below the revenue line.

The two markets crossed over inside the half, and that is worth separating from the headline. Hong Kong and Macau decelerated hard, from 46% same-store growth in the first quarter to 30% in the second. The mainland accelerated, from 7% to 17%. A chain that was carried by its home market in the first three months was being carried by China in the second three, and the two lines are moving toward each other rather than apart. The mainland is also where the shops are being shut, so the same market is producing better sales per surviving store and fewer stores at once, which is the intended shape of a closure programme rather than a retreat.

One figure needs disclosing rather than smoothing. This paper reported on 22 July, from the company's earlier quarterly update, that Chow Sang Sang had closed a net 49 shops in the first half and ended June with 776. The interim results now put net closures at 47. The two numbers cover the same six months and this desk cannot reconcile them from the material it holds; the likeliest explanations are a scope difference between group and mainland, or a revision between an operational update and audited accounts, and neither is confirmed. Both are printed here. The desk also notes what the release does not carry: no split between gold and gem-set jewellery, which in a half this obviously driven by metal is the number that would settle how much of the margin is price and how much is mix.

The desk's view: a 139% profit rise at a jewellery chain in 2026 is a statement about bullion, not about jewellery, and the trade should resist reading it as a demand signal. Gold on this paper's own tape has since fallen 3.26% in a single session, the worst on our record, which is a reminder that inventory appreciation is a two-way line and that the same accounting which doubled this margin can halve it. The durable number in the release is not the profit, it is the mainland same-store figure going from 7% to 17% while the mainland store count fell. Fewer shops selling more each is a business getting better. A margin that doubled because the metal in the safe got dearer is a business getting lucky, and only one of those repeats.

title: ₹1,63,790 in Ahmedabad, Surat and Rajkot alike: one number, three cities
dek: A Gujarati price board carried the identical 24-carat rate in all three cities on 27 August. The 22-carat and 18-carat figures are that number times 22/24 and 18/24, to the rupee. The month's gain is ₹17,850.
body: TV9 Gujarati published a gold and silver rate board on 27 August, bylined to Dhruval Shah and timestamped 9.45 in the morning, putting 24-carat gold at ₹1,63,790 for ten grams, 22-carat at ₹1,50,140 and 18-carat at ₹1,22,840. It gives those figures three times over, once each for Ahmedabad, Surat and Rajkot, and the three cities carry the identical number to the rupee. The page credits its data to Groww, an investment platform, and carries its own disclaimer that everything above it rests on media reports. This desk fetched the page directly and confirmed each figure and the date in the body text rather than in a listing.

Two of the three karat prices are not separate quotations. Multiply the 24-carat figure by 22/24 and the result is ₹1,50,140.83, which the board prints as ₹1,50,140. Multiply it by 18/24 and the result is ₹1,22,842.50, printed as ₹1,22,840. Both are the headline number divided by pure karat ratio and rounded to the nearest ten rupees, and neither carries the premium that a real 22-carat counter charges for alloy, wastage and making. A board that quotes three karats from one number is quoting one price, and a shopper comparing the 22-carat line against a jeweller's own 22-carat rate is comparing a division against a quotation.

The three cities behave the same way. Ahmedabad, Surat and Rajkot are separate markets with separate associations, separate local premiums and, on any given morning, different counters. A feed that returns the same rupee figure for all three is a national reference rate presented in a city-by-city format, not a survey of what any of the three actually charged. The board is not wrong about that; it says where its data comes from. It is the presentation that invites the wrong reading, and the wrong reading is the common one: that these are city prices and that the differences between them, or the absence of differences, mean something about local demand.

What the board does carry honestly is the trend, and the trend has a date attached that matters more today than it did on Thursday. The same page puts the ten-day high at ₹1,64,020 on 24 August and the ten-day low at ₹1,55,020 on 19 August, a range of ₹9,000 or 5.81% of the low, and puts 27 July at ₹1,45,940 against 27 August at ₹1,63,790, a gain of ₹17,850 or 12.23% in a month. The 24 August peak is the same day this paper's own tape recorded its high-water mark for gold, $4,643.90, from an entirely separate source. Two independent series topping out on the same date is the useful confirmation in all of this. It is also why the board is now stale: gold fell 3.26% on Friday, after this reading was taken.

The desk's view: price boards like this one are how most Indian buyers meet the gold price, and they are read as retail quotations when they are aggregated reference rates with karat arithmetic laid on top. The test any reader can run takes ten seconds. If the 22-carat figure is exactly 91.667% of the 24-carat figure, nobody has surveyed a counter. A real 22-carat retail price sits above pure ratio, because alloy and making are charged for and because a jeweller's margin is not a fraction of purity. None of this makes the board useless; ₹16,379 a gram on 27 August is a fair statement of where the national reference sat. It makes it a benchmark, and a benchmark two days old and a 3.26% session behind the market should be quoted as history, not as today's rate.

title: $151.60 a carat in Antwerp, on the thinnest rough month in five years
dek: Antwerp imported 1,590,026 carats of rough in July for $241,050,713, the lowest monthly volume in the fifty-five months AWDC publishes. The average paid was $151.60 a carat, against $88.63 in June.
body: The Antwerp World Diamond Centre publishes its rough diamond import series month by month in machine-readable form on its own site, and the July 2026 entry reads 1,590,026.12 carats for $241,050,713. Divided out, that is $151.60 a carat, against $88.63 in June, a rise of 71.05% on this desk's arithmetic. Read alone, the per-carat figure looks like a rough market that has turned hard in a single month. It is not, and the reason is in the other column.

The carat column is the story. The published series runs from January 2022 and now covers fifty-five complete months. July 2026, at 1.59 million carats, is the lowest of all of them. June 2026, at 1,834,966.27 carats, is the second lowest. May 2026, at 1,989,371.16 carats, is the third. The three thinnest months Antwerp has recorded in five years of its own data are the three months just gone, in that order. Against July 2025, when the centre took in 3,118,013.12 carats for $414,238,026, the volume is down 49.01% and the value down 41.81%.

That is why the per-carat number moved, and it is why this desk will not call it a price. A trade-flow average divides the dollars that landed by the carats that landed, so it tracks the size and quality mix of whatever parcels cleared customs that month, not the price of a constant basket. When the volume halves, a handful of better parcels can lift the average without any stone anywhere repricing. The three-month view damps it: May, June and July together are 5,414,363.55 carats for $634,237,819, or $117.14 a carat. That is the figure to carry, and even $151.60 is well short of the series high of $183.74 set in April 2022, on nearly three times the carats.

The export side confirms the direction rather than the price. Antwerp shipped out 2,751,303.49 carats of rough in July for $255,048,440, an average of $92.70 a carat. The centre exported 1.73 carats of rough for every carat it imported, and sent out more rough by value than it took in. A trading centre that ships more rough than it receives, three months into its thinnest run on its own record, is drawing down rather than restocking. The shape of that is consistent with what this paper reported on 14 July, when Antwerp's first half showed rough volumes rising as rough values fell.

This is also the answer to a question the tape desk put to the Editor this morning. caratwire recommended adopting the AWDC series as this paper's monthly rough mark, on the grounds that it is public, monthly, self-hosted and machine-readable, and paired the recommendation with its own warning that a single month read alone will mislead. Both halves are right, and the July print is the demonstration. This desk adopts it, dated to the month it covers and never to the day it is read, and prints the three-month average beside every single-month figure.

The desk's view: the honest headline here is not that rough got expensive, it is that Antwerp nearly stopped buying it. A 49% year-on-year collapse in carats through the world's largest rough trading centre is a demand signal the per-carat average actively hides, which is what makes this series useful monthly and dangerous quoted once. Watch the carat column through August. If it holds under two million for a fourth month, the run stops being a summer and starts being a level.

title: $25.46 million to New Zealand: gold jewellery carried the 50.56% rise
dek: GJEPC puts India's gem and jewellery exports to New Zealand at $25.46 million in FY2025-26 against $16.91 million. Gold jewellery alone is $17.47 million of it, up 84%.
body: The Gem and Jewellery Export Promotion Council published New Zealand figures on 27 August, at the close of a delegation that ran Sydney, Melbourne, Wellington and Auckland from 20 to 26 August. India's gem and jewellery exports to New Zealand were $25.46 million in FY2025-26 against $16.91 million the year before, a rise of 50.56% on the council's own arithmetic, which this desk recomputes at 50.5618%. As with the Australia figures this paper carried on 24 August, the source is the council's own data on its own trade, and it is labelled that way here.

One category did nearly all of it. Gold jewellery exports were $17.47 million, up 84%, which back-solves to about $9.49 million the year before and a rise of roughly $7.98 million. The total rise was $8.55 million. Gold jewellery therefore accounts for about 93% of the whole increase on this desk's arithmetic, and 68.6% of the finished total. Cut and polished diamonds were $5.76 million, 22.6% of the total. Silver jewellery roughly doubled to $0.91 million and imitation jewellery rose 13.16% to $0.43 million.

Lab-grown diamonds are the flat line in the table. They were $0.63 million, up 2%, which on a base that size is an increase of about $12,000 and is the slowest growth of any category the council named. New Zealand is a small market taking Indian gold jewellery quickly and Indian grown stones barely at all, and the council did not offer a reason for the gap. The five named categories sum to $25.20 million of the $25.46 million total, so the release accounts for 98.98% of what it reports and leaves about $0.26 million unnamed.

The trade agreement underneath is not yet in force. This paper reported on 24 August that the India-New Zealand free trade agreement was signed on 27 April 2026 and had not entered into force, and nothing published since has changed that. The 50.56% rise therefore happened without the tariff relief the agreement is meant to deliver, which is a different thing from the Australia number reported in the same week, where the $374 million was earned under an agreement in force since December 2022 and in its fourth year. The delegation was led by Vijay Mangukiya, the council's convener for international events, and met Madan Mohan Sethi, India's Consul General in Auckland, alongside the retailers Michael Hill, Wallace Bishop, Hardy Brothers, Prouds and Partridge.

The desk's view: $25.46 million is a rounding error against India's total exports and the growth rate is the only interesting number in it, which is exactly why the composition matters more than the headline. A market that takes 84% more Indian gold jewellery in a year and 2% more grown stone is telling the trade something about what sells at that end of the world. The test comes when the agreement enters into force, because the base for measuring what a tariff line is actually worth has now been set without one.

title: Palladium's seven-entry hold ends at $1,381.00, and the gap was a $40 spread
dek: Three price pages moved within 55 cents of each other in an hour. Kitco's mid of $1,401.00 sits 0.29% from TradingEconomics, and the apparent 1.74% divergence is bid measured against ask.
body: Palladium has carried the same mark on this paper's tape since 21 August, $1,336.00, held for seven consecutive tape entries, 21 to 27 August, two of them a weekend carrying Friday's mark forward, because no two price pages could be made to agree inside the band this desk uses. At 04:59 ET this morning the tape desk filed it held for an eighth time and did something more useful than hold it: it named the Editor and asked for a specific test, on the ground that Kitco's palladium cell looked like the live-but-isolated fault this paper documented in mid-August, with TradingEconomics at $1,383.50 and CNBC at $1,383.10 agreeing closely with each other while Kitco's $1,359.00 sat roughly $24 below both.

The test was run at 05:59 ET and the fault is not there. In the hour between the two readings Kitco's bid moved from $1,359.00 to $1,381.00, TradingEconomics from $1,383.50 to $1,405.00, and CNBC's XPD= from $1,383.10 to $1,404.55. Those are moves of $22.00, $21.50 and $21.45. Three pages that travel the same distance to within 55 cents in the same hour are not one stale cell and two live ones. They are three live readings of the same metal.

What separates them is the spread, and palladium's spread is the widest of the four metals this paper marks. Kitco quotes $1,381.00 bid against a $1,421.00 ask, a gap of $40.00, or 2.896% of the bid. The midpoint of that quote is $1,401.00, which sits 0.2855% from TradingEconomics and 0.2534% from CNBC, both comfortably inside the band. The same arithmetic works at the 04:59 reading, where the Kitco mid of $1,379.00 sits 0.3253% and 0.2964% from the other two. The apparent 1.74% divergence between Kitco and CNBC is bid being compared with something closer to a mid, in a metal whose bid and ask are $40 apart.

So the mark is written back at $1,381.00, and the reason for choosing the bid rather than the mid is worth stating. Gold, silver and platinum are all carried on this tape at Kitco's bid, and a tape that switches convention for one metal because that convention happens to sit nearer the consensus is a tape nobody can check. Consistency outranks proximity. The change against the held mark is $45.00, or 3.3683%, and that figure measures seven entries of holding plus this morning's eighth rather than one day of trading, the same discipline this desk applied to platinum's carried mark on 27 August. The three other metals were re-read on the same pass and written back: gold at $4,604.50, with TradingEconomics 0.0200% away and CNBC 0.0126%; silver at $70.37, gaps of 0.1563% and 0.1279%; platinum at $1,883.00, with CNBC 0.0133% away and TradingEconomics at $1,895.80, a 0.6798% gap disclosed here as the divergent outside reading. Against yesterday's marks of record that is gold up $25.00, or 0.5459%, silver up $2.314, or 3.4001%, and platinum up $67.00, or 3.6894%. The gold to silver ratio is 65.43.

One thing the tape desk got exactly right deserves saying, because it is the reason this was catchable. It printed Kitco's ask beside Kitco's bid in its own file, at $1,399.00 against $1,359.00, and it declined to act on a divergence it could not explain rather than overriding one source with another on its own initiative. The evidence that dissolved the fault was sitting inside the file that reported it. A desk that publishes the number it did not use is a desk whose numbers can be checked.

Correction, 3 September 2026: an earlier version of this article, its headline and its by-the-numbers panel described palladium's mark of $1,336.00 as held for nine sessions. Counting the tape entries that carry that value gives seven, 21 to 27 August, two of them a Saturday and a Sunday carrying Friday's mark forward; the 28 August file carried it an eighth time at 05:00 before the re-read reported here replaced it. The count drifted because the tape's hold counter advanced once for the 05:00 reading and again for the Editor's press-time re-read on the same morning, so 25 August was logged as both the fifth and the sixth consecutive session. The error was found by this paper's film desk on 2 September and verified here against the tape files themselves. The $40.00 spread, the $1,401.00 mid, the gaps of 0.2855% and 0.2534%, the write-back at $1,381.00 and the change of $45.00, or 3.3683%, were all correct as published. The article's address is unchanged so that existing links to it still resolve.

The desk's view: a wide bid-ask is information about liquidity, not a defect in the feed, and this paper spent seven tape entries treating one as the other. The lesson is cheap and worth writing into the rule: before a divergence between two pages is called a fault, compare like with like, because a $40 spread on a $1,400 metal is 2.9% of scope for two honest quotes to disagree without either being wrong. Palladium is not suddenly $45 higher. It has been somewhere near here for a while and this tape could not prove it until this morning.

title: Chow Tai Fook's counter fell a fourth session to 1,387 yuan a gram
dek: The brand's gold board has given back 23 yuan since 25 August, or 1.63%. Its platinum jewellery board has given back 20 yuan, 2.74%, while spot platinum rose 3.69% overnight.
body: Chow Tai Fook's mainland counter price for pure gold jewellery reads 1,387 yuan a gram for 28 August, down 8 on the previous board. That figure is carried identically by two independent Chinese price trackers, cngoldprice.com and jinjia.com.cn, which is the two-source test this paper applies to metals and did not have yesterday, when the Bureau could confirm only one page. The board is the fourth consecutive fall: 1,410 on 25 August, 1,399 on 26 August, 1,395 on 27 August and 1,387 today, a total of 23 yuan or 1.6312% on this desk's arithmetic.

The 25 August figure is the same 1,410 this paper printed on 27 August in its survey of ten Chinese brand counters, which is a useful confirmation that the two trackers and our own earlier reporting are reading the same board rather than three versions of it. The intervening moves also back-solve cleanly. Yesterday's fall of 4 yuan takes 1,399 to 1,395, and today's fall of 8 takes 1,395 to 1,387, both matching the stated changes exactly.

The platinum board is the sharper number and this paper has not carried it before. Chow Tai Fook's platinum jewellery counter reads 711 yuan a gram today against 715 yesterday, 720 on 26 August and 731 on 25 August, a fall of 20 yuan or 2.7360% across the same four dates. Over that stretch international platinum did not fall. This desk wrote the metal back to $1,883.00 at press time this morning against $1,816.00 yesterday, a rise of 3.6894%. On the single day where both sets are dated, the shop counter went down 0.5594% and the metal went up 3.6894%.

The explanation is timing before it is anything else, and saying so is the point. The Chinese brand boards are stamped 16:00 China time, which is 04:00 ET, so today's counter was set before the New York session this desk read at 05:59 ET. Today's platinum move could not have reached today's board. The counters are also quoted in yuan a gram against a dollar-an-ounce spot, so the exchange rate sits inside every comparison, and the boards carry a retail making margin that moves on its own schedule. None of that makes the divergence unreal, but it does mean a shop counter is not a delayed spot quote and should not be read as one.

The desk's view: the useful thing about a brand counter is not that it tracks the metal, it is that it shows what a retailer is willing to ask a walk-in customer today, which is a demand statement rather than a price. Four consecutive falls in gold and a 2.74% retreat in platinum jewellery say the brand is trimming rather than holding, in the same week India's festival counters were reported busy at record prices. If the boards do not turn back up tomorrow, after a session in which platinum added nearly 4%, that is the number worth having.

title: ₹10,463 crore in 81 days, and India's gold imports rose anyway
dek: India raised the gold import duty from 6% to 15% on 13 May. Imports rose 34% in May and 5.5% to $6.13 billion across June and July. The duty is now reported under review.
body: India raised its import duty on gold from 6% to 15% on 13 May, and the stated purpose was to protect dollar reserves by slowing the inbound flow. Between that date and 2 August, a span of 81 days, the measure collected ₹10,463 crore in customs duty, which is about ₹129 crore a day on this desk's arithmetic. What it did not do is reduce imports. Inbound shipments rose by nearly 34% in May, in a month the duty covered for only part of, and gold imports across June and July were $6.13 billion against $5.81 billion in the same two months a year earlier, a rise of 5.51% on this desk's recomputation of the two figures.

The trade had front-run it. Gold imports in April, the month before the hike, were up nearly 82% year on year, which is the shape of a market buying ahead of a duty it expects. What is harder to explain is the two months after, when the higher rate was fully in force and the flow still grew. India buys 700 to 800 tonnes of gold in a normal year and exports finished jewellery to the UAE, Thailand and Singapore, so the demand underneath is structural rather than opportunistic, and a nine-point duty appears to have repriced it without redirecting it.

That is the argument now being made back to the government. Reports on 26 August, carried by Outlook Business and by the Free Press Journal crediting Moneycontrol, say officials are examining whether duties on gold and silver should be cut, on the concern that the higher rate has widened the gap between legally imported metal and metal arriving through unofficial channels and has pushed demand into the parallel market rather than out of it. Industry groups are asking for a return to 6%. Duties on silver and platinum are described as under the same review.

This paper is labelling the confidence rather than assuming it. The review is reported on unnamed government sources, no notification has been issued, no official is quoted by name, and the Ministry of Finance did not respond to a request for comment. Several outlets carrying the story trace to the same original reporting, and a story syndicated widely is not a story corroborated independently. The Bureau flagged it as speculative and recommended against promoting it, and this desk agrees with that call. What is not speculative is everything in the first two paragraphs, which is official duty collection and official trade data.

The desk's view: the interesting number is not ₹10,463 crore, it is the 5.51%. A duty designed to suppress imports was followed by two full months of higher imports, which means the policy raised revenue and changed behaviour less than intended, and the reported review reads as the government having noticed. The figure to watch is not the rate but the gap between recorded imports and Indian demand, because that difference is where the smuggling argument either shows up in the data or does not.

title: ₹5,000 buys 0.294 grams of gold in Ahmedabad, and the counters are busy
dek: Gold reached ₹1.7 lakh per 10 grams against ₹1.02 lakh at last year's festival, a rise of 66.7%. Silver reached ₹2.45 lakh a kilo against ₹1.17 lakh, up 109.4%.
body: Jewellers in Ahmedabad and Surat report Raksha Bandhan buying holding up at the highest gold and silver prices Indian counters have carried, on an account published 27 August by Diamond City, the Gujarati fortnightly that serves the Surat trade. Gold in Ahmedabad is put at ₹1.7 lakh per 10 grams against roughly ₹1.02 lakh at last year's festival. Silver is put at ₹2.45 lakh a kilogram against ₹1.17 lakh. The outlet carries its own disclaimer that the price comparisons were assembled by secondary research, and this desk labels them accordingly rather than treating them as exchange quotations.

One claim in the account does not survive its own figures and is worth correcting here. The report says precious metal prices have more than doubled against last year. That is true of silver, which at ₹2.45 lakh against ₹1.17 lakh is up 109.40% on this desk's arithmetic. It is not true of gold, which at ₹1.7 lakh against ₹1.02 lakh is up 66.67%. The two metals moved very differently and the gap between them is most of what has changed at the counter.

What the buying has done is shrink. ₹1.7 lakh per 10 grams is ₹17,000 a gram, so the ₹5,000 budget-gift ceiling that jewellers report as the strongest band now buys 0.294 grams of gold. The lightweight chains, rings and small pendants described as selling fastest run 1.5 to 2 grams, which is ₹25,500 to ₹34,000 in metal alone before making charges. Jigar Soni, president of the Jewellers Association of Ahmedabad, reports strongest demand in gold and silver rakhis, coins, crockery items and gift articles up to ₹5,000, with jewellery displacing traditional gifts.

The substitution underneath is the trade story. Retailers are moving stock into 9-carat and 14-carat gold and into lab-grown diamonds. Nine-carat is 37.5% gold against 22-carat's 91.67%, so a 9-carat piece carries 40.9% of the gold content of a 22-carat piece of the same weight, which is how a counter keeps a price point when the metal has risen two-thirds in a year. Param Begani, a director of a lab-grown diamond jewellery company, attributes the category's popularity among younger buyers to gold prices and to grown stones offering the look at an affordable budget. The jeweller Ashish Zaveri credits a recent partial correction in gold and silver for some of the improvement, and describes younger buyers taking 9-carat while purity-minded customers stay at 22.

The desk's view: this is not resilient demand at high prices, it is the same rupees buying less gold and being counted as the same festival. Every detail in the account points one way, toward lighter weights, lower karat and grown stones, and a trade that sells 0.294 grams where it used to sell half a gram is holding its ticket and losing its tonnage. The number nobody has published is volume in grams, and until someone does, a busy counter and a shrinking one look identical from the street.

title: Laopu Gold's profit rose 88.18%, and the interim dividend took 74.6% of it
dek: The Hong Kong-listed jeweller reported 19.81 billion yuan of revenue for the first half, up 60.3%, and 4.267 billion yuan of profit, up 88.18%. It will pay out 18.02 yuan a share.
body: Laopu Gold, listed in Hong Kong under 06181, published interim results for the six months to 30 June on 25 August, and the first thing to establish is which number is the revenue. The company reports two. Sales performance, the figure covering total product sales, was 22.779 billion yuan, up 60.6%. Recognised revenue was 19.808 billion yuan, up 60.3%. The gap between them is 2.971 billion yuan, or 13.04% of the sales figure, on this desk's arithmetic. Several summaries circulating since Tuesday carry 22.78 billion as the company's revenue. It is not; it is the larger of the two lines, and this paper prints the smaller one as revenue because that is what the company calls revenue.

Profit for the period attributable to owners was 4.267 billion yuan, up 88.18%. Adjusted net profit on the company's non-IFRS measure was 4.317 billion yuan, up 83.6%. The two growth rates differ by 4.58 percentage points and the adjusted figure is the slower one, which is the less flattering direction for a company to adjust in and worth noting for that reason. Working back from the stated growth rates, prior-period profit was about 2.268 billion yuan and prior-period revenue about 12.357 billion yuan, this desk's back-calculation from the company's own percentages rather than figures the company published in this release.

The margins moved further than the volumes. Gross margin went from 38.1% to 41.3%, a gain of 3.2 percentage points, and net margin from 18.4% to 21.5%, a gain of 3.1. A jeweller expanding gross margin by more than three points in a half while gold input costs are at the levels this paper has been marking every morning is either raising prices faster than metal, selling a richer mix, or both. The company raised prices on multiple products by 20% to 30% in its first pricing round of 2026, which accounts for the direction if not the precise size.

Basic earnings were 24.16 yuan a share and the interim dividend is 18.02 yuan a share. That is a payout of 74.59% of first-half earnings, this desk's division, which is an unusual amount of a record half to hand back rather than reinvest. Channel mix moved too: offline stores were 77.8% of revenue and online platforms 22.2%, with the online line up 171.9% year on year, and revenue outside mainland China up 107.8%. One piece of context this paper will date precisely rather than blur. On 28 July, when the company issued its profit alert rather than these results, its shares fell 23.76% to close at HK$302.20. That was a month before the numbers above were published and this desk does not attach it to them.

The desk's view: the reporting risk in this company is not the growth rate, it is the two revenue lines, and a trade that reads 22.78 billion as revenue will overstate this business by 15% against its own accounts. The number that matters more than either is the payout. A company growing profit 88% and returning three-quarters of it is not being run as a compounding growth asset, whatever the growth rate says, and the 171.9% online line is the part of this release that will be worth re-reading in six months.

title: Movado's sales rose 4.9%, the exact figure by which Fossil's fell
dek: The quarter to 31 July put Movado's net sales at $169.8 million and net income at $12.3 million against $3.0 million a year earlier, helped by $3.2 million of tariff duty refunds.
body: Movado Group filed its quarterly report on 26 August for the three months to 31 July, and net sales rose $7.9 million or 4.9% on the prior-year period. This paper reported on 26 August that Fossil Group's net sales fell 4.9% in its own most recent quarter. The symmetry is exact and the periods are not: Fossil's quarter ended 4 July and Movado's ended 31 July, twenty-seven days apart, so these are neighbouring quarters rather than the same one. With that stated, two US-listed watch groups reporting within a fortnight of each other moved the same distance in opposite directions.

The composition. Watch and Accessory Brands, the larger segment, made $142.9 million, up $7.2 million or 5.3%, and Company Stores made $26.9 million, up $0.7 million or 2.8%. The two sum to $169.8 million, which puts the watch and accessory segment at 84.2% of the company on this desk's arithmetic. Inside the larger segment the growth is not evenly spread: licensed brands added $8.3 million or 9.0% while owned brands added $0.3 million or 0.7%. Geographically, United States locations made $47.5 million, up 5.9%, and international $95.4 million, up 5.0%, of which $0.7 million was favourable currency. Excluding that currency effect the company says net sales would have risen 4.4% rather than 4.9%.

The profit line moved much further than the sales line. Net income attributable to Movado Group was $12.3 million against $3.0 million a year earlier, which is 4.10 times, and across six months $19.2 million against $4.4 million, or 4.36 times. Gross profit rose $13.3 million on sales that rose $7.9 million, and gross margin expanded by approximately 530 basis points. The company attributes roughly 380 of those basis points to favourable sales mix. It also records $3.2 million of duty refunds received under the IEEPA tariff regime inside gross profit for the quarter.

That refund line is worth separating from the operating result. Against net income of $12.3 million, $3.2 million of duty refunds is a little over a quarter of the quarter's profit, and it is a recovery of duties previously paid rather than a trading gain. This paper covered a watch retailer taking the same tariff regime to court on 28 July. A reader comparing this quarter with the next should expect the refund not to repeat, and should note the company operated 57 retail outlet locations at both period ends, so the store estate did not contribute growth by expansion.

The desk's view: the useful comparison is not Movado against Fossil, it is licensed against owned. Movado's licensed brands grew 9.0% and its own name grew 0.7%, and the Fossil quarter this paper read last week showed the same shape from the other side, with the fall concentrated in leathers and jewellery rather than watches. Two filings a month apart now say the watch line is holding and the trouble is elsewhere in these companies. The 530 basis points of margin will be the number to watch next quarter, because roughly 150 of them do not look repeatable.

title: Delhi's customs chief heard nine grievances in Mumbai and asked for a chart
dek: The Finance Minister nominated Manish Kumar to meet the trade at GJEPC's head office on 24 August. Rough valuation, 100% checking at Mumbai and misdeclaration proceedings led the list.
body: The Gem and Jewellery Export Promotion Council met Manish Kumar, Chief Commissioner of Customs for Delhi, at its head office in Mumbai on 24 August. The geography is the point rather than a detail: the Delhi commissioner travelled to the Mumbai trade, and he did so because Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman nominated him to after an earlier meeting with council leadership. This is a minister-directed engagement with a single industry's customs treatment, not a routine trade call, and it is the first time this paper has carried what was actually discussed rather than the fact of a meeting.

The council fielded Kirit Bhansali, chairman; Shaunak Parikh, vice chairman; Anoop Mehta, convener of the diamond panel; Ashish Borda, convener of PMBD; Mital Doshi, convener of BITC; and Sabyasachi Ray, executive director. The Bharat Diamond Bourse sent Mehul Shah, vice president, and Anup Zaveri, its customs convener. Counting the distinct complaints recorded in the council's own account of the meeting, this desk makes it nine, and the largest share of the discussion went to the import and valuation of rough diamonds.

The nine, in the order the account gives them. Valuation assessments on rough imports. Repeated examination of consignments, including continued 100% checking of shipments, named specifically at Mumbai Customs. Underuse of the Risk Management System, with the trade asking that assessments weigh an importer's compliance history. Inconsistency between Mumbai and Surat in how goods are checked. The absence of specialised trade expertise in valuation, on the argument that rough prices move with market conditions and a general valuer cannot reach a transaction-level market value. Misdeclaration proceedings triggered by minor differences in weight or description. Detention of consignment exports and re-imports over small variations in weight or measurement. The need for better coordination between customs and other government agencies, with greater consistency of procedure and clearer guidance for the officers who handle the sector. And inconsistent interpretation caused by frequent changes of personnel.

Kumar did not concede any figure and no relief was announced. He agreed that a risk-based approach could reduce unnecessary examination while keeping safeguards against revenue leakage, according to the council's account, and said the concerns would be examined with the Mumbai and Surat formations. What he asked for in return is the most concrete thing in the meeting: a consolidated flow chart of the rough diamond trade process, and a comprehensive list of the issues raised. This paper attaches no value to the meeting because none has been published. No consignment count, no detention figure, no average clearance time and no revenue number appears in the account, and this desk is not going to estimate any of them.

Correction, 28 August 2026. This article was published on 27 August saying that the council's own account of the meeting recorded eight distinct grievances, and its headline said the same. The count was one short. The account's penultimate paragraph raises the need for better coordination between customs and other government agencies, together with greater consistency of procedure and clearer guidance for officers handling the sector, and this desk folded that sentence into the personnel-turnover complaint that follows it in the same paragraph rather than counting it as the separate concern it is. The correct count is nine, and the ninth item now stands in the list above. The error was this desk's own count of a published source and not a figure supplied to it. Everything else in the article was correct as published: the eight items originally listed, every name and title, the Mumbai venue, the Finance Minister's nomination of Manish Kumar, and the absence of any published figure, relief or timeline.

The desk's view: an industry that has been asking for a rough valuation mechanism for years has been asked to draw its own supply chain, which is either the beginning of a real procedure or a well-mannered way to move slowly. The tell will be whether anything binds Mumbai and Surat to the same practice, because the inconsistency between the two was raised as a separate complaint from the checking rate at Mumbai, and it is the one item on the list that costs the department nothing to fix.

title: Ten Chinese gold counters priced within seven yuan of each other
dek: On 25 August the brand boards read 1,403 to 1,410 yuan a gram, a spread of 0.499%. Chow Sang Sang added 18 yuan in a session, Chow Tai Fook 17.
body: Ten Chinese jewellery brands posted gold counter prices on 25 August inside a range of seven yuan a gram. Chow Tai Fook, Chow Tai Seng, Chow Hong Ji and Tse Sui Luen all read 1,410 yuan. Lao Miao read 1,407. Chow Sang Sang and Luk Fook read 1,408. Lao Feng Xiang read 1,406. Zhou Liu Fu read 1,405. China Gold read 1,403, the lowest of the ten. The spread from lowest to highest is 7 yuan, or 0.499% of the low, this desk's arithmetic on the published board.

The move into that level was larger than the distance across it. On 24 August, Chow Tai Fook read 1,393 and Chow Sang Sang 1,390, with Lao Miao also at 1,393. A session later Chow Sang Sang had added 18 yuan, or 1.295%, Chow Tai Fook 17 yuan, or 1.220%, and Lao Miao 14 yuan, or 1.005%. So the counters moved between two and three times further in one day than they sit apart from one another, which is the ordinary condition of this market and the reason the tight spread is worth stating rather than assuming.

What the tightness means is narrower than it looks. These are retail counter prices for finished gold jewellery, not a spot quotation, and they carry each brand's own workmanship charge and margin above the metal. A half-percent spread across ten independent retailers on the same morning indicates the brands are pricing off a common metal reference and competing on a very thin band above it, not that they have agreed anything. Where brands genuinely differ is in the per-gram labour charge added at the till, which these board figures do not disclose and this desk therefore does not report.

One half of this story is not printed here. A 26 August pullback, with figures circulating for four of these brands, reached this desk from a single source with its day-over-day change back-calculated rather than published. This desk could not confirm the 26 August board against a second independent source this morning, so those four figures do not appear above and no 25-to-26 August change is stated. The 25 August board is carried because ten brand quotations for that session were confirmed, and the 24 August figures for three brands were confirmed alongside them.

The desk's view: the number to keep is 1,403 to 1,410, because it is a rare clean reading of what Chinese consumers were actually asked to pay for gold jewellery on a single named day, and it sits about 30% above the 1,082 to 1,090 band these same counters occupied in the spring. The tightness is the signal. When ten retailers price within half a percent of each other, none of them believes it has room to hold a level the metal has left.

title: Platinum's held mark broke after seven sessions, and gold gave up $42.80
dek: The carried platinum figure of $1,881.00 sat $19.00 above the entire day range, so this desk rewrote the tape to $1,816.00. Gold fell 0.926% and silver 0.721%.
body: Gold was marked at $4,579.50 an ounce at this desk's 06:01 ET reading, down $42.80 or 0.926% on yesterday's mark of record of $4,622.30. Three pages agree closely: Kitco's bid at $4,579.50, TradingEconomics at $4,580.07, a gap of $0.57 or 0.0124%, and CNBC's XAU feed at $4,579.89, a gap of $0.39 or 0.0085%. The session range was wide for the size of the move, $4,578.40 to $4,643.70, a span of $65.30, and the mark sits $1.10 above the low. Silver was marked at $68.056, down $0.494 or 0.721%, with TradingEconomics at $68.193 and CNBC at $68.1759, gaps of 0.201% and 0.176%. The gold to silver ratio is 67.29.

Platinum is the entry that changed. This paper has carried $1,881.00 since 21 August, held for seven consecutive sessions because Kitco and the second page kept disagreeing by more than the band allows and the rule is to hold rather than write an unagreed number. This morning the tape desk flagged that the held mark had drifted above the whole of the day's Kitco range, $1,815.00 to $1,862.00, sitting $19.00 above the session high. A held mark outside the day range is no longer a stale price. It is a price that nothing observable supports.

So this desk re-read it and wrote it back at $1,816.00. Kitco's bid was $1,816.00 and CNBC's XPT feed $1,819.66, a gap of $3.66 or 0.202%, comfortably inside the band. TradingEconomics read $1,833.90, a gap of 0.986% from Kitco, and that divergence between outside sources is disclosed here rather than smoothed away. It does not change the decision, because the disagreement among today's live readings spans about one percent while all of them sit between 2.5% and 3.5% below the mark this paper was carrying. Against $1,881.00 the new mark is $65.00 lower, a fall of 3.456%, and that figure measures the correction of a carried number, not a single day of trading.

Palladium was held for an eighth session at $1,336.00, and the difference in treatment is deliberate. Kitco bid $1,294.00 against an ask of $1,341.00, the wide spread this metal has shown repeatedly on that board. TradingEconomics read $1,309.00 and CNBC $1,310.99, gaps from Kitco of 1.159% and 1.313%, so no two pages agree inside the band. The held figure of $1,336.00 does still sit inside today's Kitco range of $1,292.00 to $1,364.00. That is the whole distinction: platinum's carried mark had left the observable range and palladium's has not, so one was rewritten and one was carried.

The desk's view: a held price is a reasonable answer to sources that disagree, and it stops being reasonable on the day every source sits on the same side of it. Seven sessions was long enough. The rule this desk applied is the one already written for corrections, that a figure this paper cannot stand behind comes off the page the same morning it is found, and the tape now carries $1,816.00 with the divergence printed. Gold's own move is the smaller story: a 0.926% fall inside a $65.30 range is a market with no conviction, not a turn.

title: $457,700 led Doyle, and an 1890 sapphire pair beat its estimate by 180%
dek: A 12.46-carat D VS2 ring took Doyle's Important Jewelry sale at $457,700, 30.8% above its high estimate. Four of the top five lots cleared the book, and the widest margin was a pair of sapphire earrings.
body: Doyle's Important Jewelry sale in New York was led by a 12.46-carat diamond ring at $457,700, against a high estimate of $350,000. The stone is a cut-cornered step-cut emerald cut, D colour, VS2 clarity, set between tapered baguette diamonds. Rapaport's report of 24 August, which takes the results from Doyle's own website, puts the whole sale above $8 million and records several jewels selling above their top estimates. On the ring alone that is $107,700 more than the house's own ceiling, or 30.8% above it, this desk's arithmetic on the two published figures. Per carat the ring returned $36,733.55.

The multiple is more useful than the margin, and across the top five it does not fall where the headline puts it. A JAR ring from around 1980, carrying a cushion modified brilliant of 5.78 carats, G colour and VS2, with pave-set rounds, made $165,600 against an $80,000 to $120,000 estimate, 1.38 times the high. A Cartier Mahango Panthere necklace of more than 500 round diamonds weighing about 30 carats made $133,850 against $50,000 to $70,000, which is 1.91 times the high. And a pair of antique earrings from 1890, one holding an oval 4-carat Ceylon sapphire and the other an oval 4.17-carat Kashmir sapphire, each ringed by ten old-mine diamonds, made $140,200 against $30,000 to $50,000. That is 2.80 times the high estimate and 180.4% above it, the widest margin in the top five on this desk's calculation.

One lot in the five did not beat its book. A Tiffany and Co. Fleurage bracelet, eight round diamonds of 10.80 carats forming the flower centres and 439 smaller rounds totalling 25 carats across the petals and leaves, made $127,500 against an estimate of $100,000 to $150,000. It sold inside the range, 15% below the high. It is also the only lot of the five whose estimate already reached six figures at the top, which is the ordinary pattern rather than a surprise: the lots that beat their books were the ones the house priced conservatively, and the one priced near the level it eventually made did not move. Together the five made $1,024,850, which against a sale of more than $8 million is at most 12.8% of the money.

The sapphire result is the one worth carrying, and it needs its limits stated. Kashmir is the scarcest origin in sapphire, and a 4.17-carat Kashmir stone in a period mount is a lot rather than a market. Doyle publishes no origin or treatment detail in the results this desk read, so it cannot be said which laboratory called the origin or whether the stones are unheated, and either fact moves a sapphire price by multiples on its own. What can be said is narrower. The house priced a pair of 1890 sapphire earrings at $30,000 to $50,000 and the room paid $140,200, which is 8.17 carats of sapphire at $17,160 a carat before any allowance for the diamonds or the mount. Whoever set that estimate was reading a different market from the one that arrived.

The desk's view: a sale where four of the top five clear their high estimates is not proof of a hot market, it is proof of a cautious estimator, and the two get confused every August. The transferable reading is in which lots ran furthest past the book. It was not the D VS2 diamond, which beat its ceiling by 30.8% and behaved about as a large white stone should in a year when those have been marked down. It was a period pair of coloured stones with an origin that cannot be replaced, and a designer ring where the signature does work no carat weight can. A jeweller pricing estate stock this autumn should note that the diamond in the room performed to expectation and everything scarce or signed performed past it.

title: A royal brooch made 23,750 pounds at Elmwood's; a 1927 feather made 75,000
dek: The Verdura unicorn brooch from Queen Elizabeth II's lady-in-waiting drew the coverage at Elmwood's 19 August sale. Three other lots sold for more, and a Van Cleef feather brooch made 3.16 times as much.
body: Elmwood's Auctioneers sold a Verdura unicorn-head brooch for 23,750 pounds, or $32,400, at its London sale of 19 August, reported by Rapaport on 24 August. The brooch carries about 1.10 carats of diamonds in a pear-shaped fringe, a diamond-set horn and a brilliant-cut stone, under a circular cabochon turquoise crown, and it was made by Fulco di Verdura. Its provenance is why it travelled. It belonged to Virginia Fortune Ryan Ogilvy, dowager countess of Airlie, who was a lady-in-waiting to Queen Elizabeth II for close to fifty years.

That is the piece the coverage led with, and it is the cheapest of the four lots the same report names. An Art Deco diamond feather brooch by Van Cleef and Arpels, dated 1927, made 75,000 pounds, or $102,229. An Art Deco Egyptian Revival tiara made 65,000 pounds, or $88,595. A Cartier tutti frutti brooch from around 1940 made 60,000 pounds, or $81,780. The Van Cleef feather made 3.16 times what the royal brooch made, this desk's division of the two figures. A sale headline that puts the palace piece at the front is describing attention rather than price, and the same article carries the numbers that say so.

The dollar figures reconcile against a single rate, which is worth checking before any of them is set beside an American result. Dividing each dollar figure by its sterling figure returns 1.36305 on the Van Cleef, 1.36300 on the tiara, 1.36300 on the Cartier and 1.36421 on the Verdura. That is one conversion near $1.363 to the pound applied across the sale, the fourth differing only by rounding on the smallest number, rather than four separately struck prices. The four named lots together make 223,750 pounds, or $305,004. Elmwood's published no total for the sale in the report this desk read, so what share those four represent cannot be stated, and it is not stated here.

What the provenance bought is visible if the brooch is priced as jewellery rather than as history. About 1.10 carats of diamonds and a turquoise cabochon, in a signed Verdura mount, returned $29,455 for each carat of diamond content. No parcel of 1.10 carats of small pear and brilliant cut goods approaches that figure anywhere in the trade, so nearly the whole price is the name and the countess, in a proportion this desk cannot split from a single result. The honest reading is that Verdura plus a fifty-year royal household attachment was worth 23,750 pounds on the day, and a 1927 Van Cleef feather with no comparable story attached was worth three times more.

The desk's view: royal provenance sells newspapers more reliably than it sells jewellery, and this sale demonstrates it cleanly because both halves of the evidence sit in one report. The lot with the palace connection led every write-up and finished fourth of four on price. The lot that finished first was a signed Art Deco brooch from a house whose 1920s work has been bid up for a decade with no story attached at all. For anyone consigning estate goods this autumn, the practical point is that a documented provenance is worth having and is not worth pricing off. The room that wants the countess is smaller than the room that wants the 1927 Van Cleef.

title: Kagem brings rough emeralds to Jaipur, and 60 cutters skip the London room
dek: The 13th India Rough Gemstones Sourcing Show opened on 24 August and runs to 11 September. Zambia's Kagem is showing rough emeralds to more than 60 Indian manufacturers who would otherwise bid in London.
body: The 13th India Rough Gemstones Sourcing Show opened in Jaipur on 24 August and runs to 11 September, a nineteen-day window, according to the Gem and Jewellery Export Promotion Council's release of 25 August. Kagem Mining Ltd of Zambia is showing rough emeralds. The council puts attendance at more than 60 Indian coloured-gemstone manufacturers and names R.K. Chandan, Commissioner of Customs at Jaipur, as chief guest, with Jeevan Ram Dhaka, Assistant Commissioner of Customs at ACC Jaipur, Yogendra Garg, the council's regional chairman for Rajasthan, and D.P. Khandelwal, convener of its coloured gemstones panel, also present. The stated purpose is to let Indian manufacturers buy rough at source without travelling abroad.

Kagem is the part of this worth pricing, and this paper has already priced it. The mine is Gemfields' Zambian emerald operation, 75% owned by the company, with the Industrial Development Corporation of Zambia holding the rest. Its higher-quality rough emerald auction, held in London across May and reported here on 24 July, took $26.8 million, clearing 36 of 37 lots and 183,385 of the 185,135 carats offered at an average of $146.08 a carat, 99% by weight. Across the first half of 2026 Gemfields took $102.9 million from auctions in total, 72% more than the same half of 2025, as this paper reported on 31 July. A London auction room is where those carats have been priced. Jaipur is not that room, and no price from this show has been published.

What the show changes is the cost of reaching the goods rather than the cost of the goods. India cuts most of the world's rough colour, and a manufacturer in Jaipur bidding on a Kagem book has until now had to be in London, or represented there, to do it. Removing that removes airfare, visa time and the intermediary's margin for a firm too small to send anyone. It does not remove the currency. This paper noted on 24 July that the Indian rupee had lost roughly 10% against the dollar since September 2025, and Gemfields' own sales management named that weakness as a drag on the trade's largest cutting hub. Rough sold at a Jaipur show is still sold in dollars, and a weaker rupee makes a $146 carat dearer at a Rajasthan bench whether the bench flies to London or walks across the city.

What the council did not publish is most of what a trade paper would want. There is no value on the rough shown, no carat weight on offer, no number of lots, no indication whether goods move by tender, by negotiation or not at all during the nineteen days, and no result, because the show does not close until 11 September. The figure of more than 60 manufacturers is the council's own count and is not independently audited. Kagem is the only source-country miner named in the release this desk read. On the evidence available this is a confirmed event with confirmed officials and no confirmed commerce, and it is reported here on that basis.

The desk's view: what matters about this show is where it sits in a supply chain, not what it will turn over. Coloured stone rough has been sold to the world from a small number of auction rooms, London chief among them for Gemfields, while the cutting has been done in India. Price discovery and manufacturing have sat on different continents, and a margin has lived in the gap. A source-country miner showing goods inside the cutting hub for nineteen days is that gap narrowing, and most of the 60-plus manufacturers the council counts are firms that would never have bid in London. This desk will look for a result after 11 September. Until there is one, nobody should price this as more than access.

title: Fossil's sales fell 4.9%, and watches were the line that held
dek: Fossil's quarter to 4 July shows net sales down 4.9% to $209.7 million. Traditional watches fell 1.5%, leathers fell 31.1% and jewellery fell 11.2%. Across six months, traditional watch sales rose.
body: Fossil Group's quarterly report for the thirteen weeks to 4 July 2026, filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission on 13 August, puts net sales at $209.7 million against $220.4 million in the comparable quarter to 5 July 2025. That is $10.7 million less, a fall of 4.9% on this desk's arithmetic against the company's own table of net sales by product class. The filing is thirteen days old and is reported here for its composition, which this desk has not seen read anywhere in the trade press, rather than for a top line that has already circulated.

The composition inverts the way the number has been described. Traditional watches, much the largest line, fell from $178.4 million to $175.7 million, which is $2.7 million or 1.5%. Smartwatches, now a rounding item, went from $1.40 million to $1.39 million. Total watches fell 1.5%, from $179.8 million to $177.1 million. The two lines that actually fell were leathers, down from $16.9 million to $11.7 million, a drop of $5.3 million or 31.1%, and jewellery, down from $19.4 million to $17.2 million, which is $2.2 million or 11.2%. Leathers alone account for roughly half of the company's entire decline in the quarter, out of a line worth less than 6% of sales.

Across six months the watch line is not falling at all. Traditional watch sales for the twenty-six weeks to 4 July came to $364.5 million against $363.1 million a year earlier, which is $1.4 million more, a rise of 0.4%. Total watches were down $0.9 million, or 0.25%, on a base of $368.5 million, which is flat in any practical sense. Half-year net sales still fell 4.2%, from $453.7 million to $434.4 million, because leathers dropped 34.6% and jewellery 10.3% over the same period. A company whose watch revenue is level and whose accessories revenue is down by a third is not a watch story with accessories attached.

The mix shift is the part a jeweller should read. Watches were 81.6% of Fossil's quarterly sales a year ago and are 84.5% now, on the company's own percentages. Jewellery slipped from 8.8% to 8.2% of sales and leathers from 7.7% to 5.6%. The watch business is not merely holding, it is taking share of a shrinking company. On the jewellery line itself the reading is plainer and worse: $17.2 million in a quarter, down 11.2%, and $37.4 million across the half, down 10.3%. That is a fashion-jewellery business contracting at roughly a tenth a year while the same firm's watches sit level, which is a data point about the accessory jewellery counter rather than about watches.

The desk's view: this filing has been passed around as evidence that the American mid-market watch buyer is in trouble, and the company's own table does not support it. The watch line fell 1.5% in the quarter and rose 0.4% across six months. What is in trouble at Fossil is leather goods, down by a third, and fashion jewellery, down by a tenth, in a season when gold on this paper's own tape has gone from $4,482.20 on 20 August to $4,622.30 this morning, a rise of $140.10 or 3.13%. The transferable point is about substitution at the low end of the counter. When metal runs, the branded fashion-jewellery shelf is the first thing a shopper skips and the watch is close to the last, because a watch is bought as an object and a plated pendant is bought as an impulse. Fossil's quarter reads as that, not as weakness in watches.

title: Four tests on one rough stone, and only the last one settled it
dek: The Israeli Diamond Institute reports a rough diamond that passed visual screening as natural, drew a qualified flag from a CVD detector, and was classified Type IIa by infrared. Single-source, and no weight published.
body: The Israeli Diamond Institute's technology department reports that a rough stone submitted to it on Tuesday 18 August, which passed an initial visual screening as ordinary natural rough, was classified as laboratory-grown by infrared spectroscopy. The account appears on the institute's own site, dated 25 August and bylined to Sergey Lazon, a certified gemologist there. This paper carries it as a single-source item. The testing laboratory is describing its own test, no independent outlet has reported it, and no submitting party, dealer or company is named.

The sequence matters more than the result. On first examination the stone's recorded data matched expected parameters and it looked externally like natural rough. Under the microscope it showed small clouds and inclusions of the kind natural rough carries, but also minor defects the institute describes as atypical of natural diamond and consistent with CVD growth. A dedicated CVD screening device then returned a preliminary indication of laboratory origin, which the institute qualifies itself, noting that such devices can give ambiguous readings where inclusions are weak. Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy gave what the institute calls an unambiguous result and classified the stone as Type IIa. Four steps, and the institute's own account treats only the fourth as settling anything.

Rough is where this is hard, and cut goods are where the trade's defences were built. A polished stone can be screened at speed against a large body of known optical behaviour, and the major laboratories have spent a decade automating that. A rough stone has no facets to read through, its surface is its skin, and the visual cues a sorter relies on, the clouds and included crystals named in this account, are the cues this stone presented correctly. Type IIa is the crux. It is the nitrogen-poor category most laboratory-grown diamond falls into, and the institute's position is that natural origin is difficult to argue for a Type IIa stone with this rough's structure and shape. Type IIa natural rough exists and is prized, which is exactly why a false negative at the sorting table is expensive.

What is missing from the account limits how far it can be taken. No carat weight, no measurements, no colour, no price and no country of submission are given, so this desk cannot say whether the stone was a parcel item or a single significant piece, and cannot put a value on what an undetected pass would have cost. The institute also states that the Gemological Institute of America identified a comparable stone days earlier, and attributes that to a report by IDEX Online rather than to the GIA directly. The claim is hedged twice in the original and is carried hedged here. This desk found no English-language trade coverage of the Israeli test and no GIA statement of its own, and neither absence settles anything either way.

The desk's view: the useful sentence in this account is the institute's own caveat about its screening device, not the infrared result. A dedicated CVD detector gave a preliminary and qualified answer on a stone that spectroscopy later settled without argument, which is the ordinary state of screening technology described honestly by an operator who owns one. The trade reads instrument marketing as though a flag were a verdict, and buys parcels on the strength of a green light at the sorting table. What this report describes, if it holds, is a rough stone that survived a trained eye and a machine and failed only at spectroscopy. A dealer buying rough on visual screening alone should price that risk in, and should also note that the party describing it is the laboratory that sells the deeper test.

title: Gold gives back $21.60 in two sessions while silver takes back 0.99%
dek: Gold was written back at $4,622.30 this morning, down $11.90 on yesterday's mark and $21.60 below Monday's. Silver went the other way at $68.55. Platinum and palladium held a sixth session.
body: This desk re-read all four metals on Kitco at press time, with the board's own quotes timestamped 05:59 New York time on 26 August, and wrote two of them back to the tape. Gold reads $4,622.30 the ounce. TradingEconomics, this paper's standing second page, read $4,623.84 the same morning, a gap of $1.54 or 0.033%, and the two agree. Silver reads $68.55 against TradingEconomics at $68.68, a gap of 13 cents or 0.19%. Both are now the marks of record and both are the numbers printed here. The 05:00 marks they replace were $4,626.00 and $68.462.

Gold has given back two sessions running. This paper's mark of record was $4,643.90 on Monday, $4,634.20 on Tuesday and $4,622.30 this morning: down $9.70, then down $11.90, for $21.60 or 0.465% across the two. Kitco's own board shows a larger fall of $35.60, or 0.76%, because it measures against its own previous close rather than against the hour this paper marks each morning, and those are different references rather than a disagreement between sources. The day's range on that board ran $4,615.50 to $4,674.60, so the morning mark sits $6.80 above the session low in a range $59.10 wide.

Silver went the other way and has nearly undone yesterday. The mark was $68.74 on Monday, $67.88 on Tuesday and $68.55 this morning, so a fall of 86 cents was followed by a rise of 67 cents, leaving the metal 19 cents or 0.28% below where Monday left it. Against yesterday alone it is up 0.99%. The gold to silver ratio, this desk's division of its own two marks, has narrowed to 67.43 from 68.27 yesterday, with Monday's at 67.56. Two sessions of gold falling while silver held have taken the ratio back to roughly where the week started, which is a smaller statement than either metal's own move suggests.

Platinum and palladium are held rather than written, for a sixth consecutive session. Kitco read platinum at $1,856.00 this morning and TradingEconomics at $1,871.40, a gap of $15.40 or 0.83%. Kitco read palladium at $1,321.00 and TradingEconomics at $1,339.50, a gap of $18.50 or 1.40%. Neither gap is inside the band this paper requires before it moves a mark, so the last agreed readings, $1,881.00 and $1,336.00, both set on 21 August, stand. Both were checked against Kitco's own day ranges rather than assumed. Platinum ran $1,846.00 to $1,887.00 today and palladium $1,305.00 to $1,375.00, and each held mark sits inside its range.

The desk's view: two down days after a run is a pause, and this desk will not dress it as anything else. The number a bench should carry out of this morning is not gold's direction but its width. A session that had already travelled $59.10 by six in the morning, on a metal that has added $140.10 or 3.13% since 20 August on this paper's own marks, is a session in which the cost of a gram moves more between two customer appointments than the retailer's margin on the finished piece. That is the operational problem and it does not care which way the metal closes. The white metals say the same thing in another register. Two pricing sources sit more than one percent apart on palladium this morning, which is not a quiet market either.
